[#TGT:477b207547388eb5] Accordingly, the compliance outcome is that proportional-share inclusion determines how much of the related undertaking’s data is brought into the consolidation, while the netting requirement determines how that data must be presented for the consolidated group own-funds calculation—i.e., after removing intra-group transaction effects from the relevant data inputs. [#SRC:907d8b8e4af834c2] [#TGT:477b207547388eb5]","For the purposes of the calculation of the consolidated group own funds , the data referred to in 11.1A and 11.1B shall be net of any intra-group transaction .","Notwithstanding point (4) of 11.1A data of related undertakings linked by a common management relationship shall be included in accordance with points (1), (3), (4), (5) or (6) of 11.1A on the basis of the proportional share as referred to in Chapter 8 .",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,907d8b8e4af834c2,477b207547388eb5,,,907d8b8e4af834c2,477b207547388eb5,,,,,HV0101,d0307902f53d75e0,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

d2f7d3287e9cb100,"If a derivative has several important risk drivers, when do you map it to one risk category versus several, and what do you need to be ready to show the competent authorities about the hedging sets for those categories?","You need to (1) map the derivative to the right risk category or categories based on its material risk drivers, and (2) be able to provide specific hedging-set information by risk category if the competent authorities ask. [#SRC:83d0ae2a5dfdf3ce] If all the material risk drivers for the derivative fall in the same risk category, you map the transaction only once to that category, using the most material risk driver as the basis. [#TGT:28d975e9bccdd9ad] If the material risk drivers fall into different risk categories, you map the transaction once to each risk category where it has at least one material risk driver, and you use the most material risk driver within each category for that mapping. [#TGT:28d975e9bccdd9ad] After hedging sets are established for each risk category, you must be able to provide, on request: how many hedging sets exist in each risk category; the primary or most material risk driver for the relevant transactions (or, where applicable, the pair of risk drivers for each hedging set); and how many transactions are in each hedging set. [#SRC:83d0ae2a5dfdf3ce]","Institutions shall make available upon request by the competent authorities the number of hedging sets established in accordance with paragraph 2 of this Article for each risk category, with the primary risk driver, or the most material risk driver in the given risk category for transactions referred to in Article 277(3) , or the pair of risk drivers of each of those hedging sets and with the number of transactions in each of those hedging sets .","By way of derogation from paragraph 2 , institutions shall map derivative transactions that have more than one material risk driver to more than one risk category. Where all the material risk drivers of one of those transactions belong to the same risk category, institutions shall only be required to map that transaction once to that risk category on the basis of the most material of those risk drivers. Where the material risk drivers of one of those transactions belong to different risk categories, institutions shall map that transaction once to each risk category for which the transaction has at least one material risk driver, on the basis of the most material of the risk drivers in that risk category.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,83d0ae2a5dfdf3ce,28d975e9bccdd9ad,,,83d0ae2a5dfdf3ce,28d975e9bccdd9ad,,,,,HV0102,d2f7d3287e9cb100,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

9f6a43f2eec1dad8,"When a firm is maintaining the transitional measure on technical provisions over the transitional period, under what circumstances may it recalculate the measure more frequently than the standard interval, and where is the PRA’s clarification on the recalculation process made available online?","A firm may recalculate the transitional measure on technical provisions (TMTP) on a regular cycle of every 24 months, but it can do so more often if the firm’s risk profile has materially changed; this reflects the Directive approach that is described as being transposed into HM Treasury’s Solvency 2 Regulations 2015 and is the baseline against which the PRA sets its expectations for maintaining TMTP over the transitional period and handling recalculations. [#SRC:f12971ae475fa040] The PRA’s clarification is provided through a supervisory statement intended to explain the PRA’s expectations on maintaining TMTP and the recalculation process, and the online location for the November 2016 update to that supervisory statement is the Bank of England PRA webpage at www.bankofengland.co.uk/pra/Pages/publications/ss/2016/ss1715update.aspx. [#TGT:8db537fa9d23cb87] In practice, to align with these expectations, the firm should treat the 24‑month interval as the default recalculation cadence while being prepared to justify a more frequent recalculation by demonstrating that a material change in its risk profile has occurred, and it should consult the referenced online supervisory statement update for the PRA’s clarifications on process and maintenance over the transitional period. [#SRC:f12971ae475fa040] [#TGT:8db537fa9d23cb87]","The Solvency II Directive allows for a recalculation of the transitional measure on technical provisions (TMTP) 1 every 24 months, or more frequently where the risk profile of the firm has materially changed. These Directive provisions have been transposed by HM Treasury’s Solvency 2 Regulations 2015 (2015/575) (see Regulation 54) 2 . The purpose of this supervisory statement is to provide clarity with respect to the PRA’s expectations as to how the TMTP should be maintained over the transitional period and the process for recalculations of the TMTP. It should be read alongside Regulation 54 of the Solvency 2 Regulations 2015, the Transitional Measures Part of the PRA Rulebook and the Supervisory Statement 17/15 ‘Solvency II: transitional measures on risk-free interest rates and technical provisions’ 3 .",3. November 2016: www.bankofengland.co.uk/pra/Pages/publications/ss/2016/ss1715update.aspx,DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,f12971ae475fa040,8db537fa9d23cb87,,,f12971ae475fa040,8db537fa9d23cb87,,,,,HV0103,9f6a43f2eec1dad8,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

05e60eb208924d28,"If the scheme’s funds once hit the target level but later fall to under two-thirds of that target, what does the FSCS have to do about levies—and how does that fit with the need to pay back any money it borrowed under the loan arrangements?","If the deposit guarantee scheme’s available financial means have reached the target level for the first time and then later fall to less than two-thirds of that target, the FSCS must impose regular DGS compensation cost levies on DGS members at a level that lets the scheme reach the target level again within six years. [#TGT:c7ca74e274b138ba] Separately, when the FSCS has borrowed amounts under the referenced borrowing arrangements, it must impose a DGS compensation costs levy on DGS members that is large enough to repay what was borrowed within a reasonable time, and it must meet the repayment deadlines in the applicable loan agreement (and the referenced related provision). [#SRC:6bd5528a11ff8d7e] Put together, the FSCS needs to set levies so they achieve both outcomes at the same time: rebuilding the scheme’s funds back to the target level within the six-year window triggered by the drop below two-thirds, while also ensuring the borrowed amounts are repaid on the loan agreement’s timetable and within a reasonable time. [#TGT:c7ca74e274b138ba] [#SRC:6bd5528a11ff8d7e]",The FSCS must impose a DGS compensation costs levy on DGS members sufficient to repay any amounts borrowed in accordance with 32.2 within a reasonable time and in accordance with repayment deadlines under the applicable loan agreement and 34.3 .,"(1) If, after the available financial means of the deposit guarantee scheme have reached the target level for the first time, the available financial means have been reduced to less than two-thirds of the target level , the FSCS must impose regular DGS compensation cost levies on DGS members at a level allowing the target level to be reached again within six years.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,6bd5528a11ff8d7e,c7ca74e274b138ba,,,6bd5528a11ff8d7e,c7ca74e274b138ba,,,,,HV0104,05e60eb208924d28,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

0245ac9fe25ebe1b,"When a firm is valuing with-profits policy liabilities, under what circumstances must it move away from a retrospective calculation and instead use a prospective calculation, and what is the required prospective valuation method for the liabilities that fall within scope?","A firm must switch from a retrospective calculation to a prospective calculation when the retrospective approach would not adequately reflect the value of the with-profits policy liabilities, or when the firm can demonstrate that using the retrospective approach is not practicable; in assessing practicability and appropriateness, the PRA expects the firm to consider the nature of its with-profits policies and whether the retrospective results would be meaningful, with whole of life policies (or other policies where a retrospective result could be negative or materially lower than a prospective value) given as examples where a prospective approach might be needed. [#SRC:681709c2b6db278a] When those circumstances apply, the firm must calculate the value of its with-profits policy liabilities on a prospective basis for the liabilities in scope (excluding future policy-related liabilities). [#TGT:4234a0c42c171b96] The prospective calculation must be performed as an aggregate across each with-profits policy, using the net present values of the expected future cash-flows specified for that purpose. [#TGT:4234a0c42c171b96]","Surplus Funds 3.2 generally requires the value of with-profits policy liabilities to be calculated on the basis of a retrospective approach set out in Surplus Funds 3.3 . However, where this approach would not adequately reflect the value of the liabilities, or the firm is able to demonstrate that this approach is not practicable, then the prospective basis for calculation in Surplus Funds 3.4 is required. The PRA expects firms to consider whether the application of the retrospective approach would be practicable given the nature of their with-profits policies and, even if possible, whether the results would be meaningful or an appropriate basis for the calculations. While each firm will need to consider its own specific circumstances, whole of life policies or other policies where the result of the retrospective calculation might be negative or significantly lower than the value calculated using the prospective approach are examples where the prospective approach might be necessary.","Where the circumstances set out in 3.2 apply, a firm must calculate the value of its with-profits policy liabilities (other than future policy-related liabilities ) on a prospective basis as the aggregate of the net present values of the following expected future cash-flows in respect of each with-profits policy :",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,681709c2b6db278a,4234a0c42c171b96,,,681709c2b6db278a,4234a0c42c171b96,,,,,HV0105,0245ac9fe25ebe1b,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

a9cf7943a6f83fe5,"For a CTP operational incident, what is the timing and trigger for a critical third party to provide incident information initially versus providing further information after later developments (including when the incident is resolved), and who must receive the later updates?","A critical third party has two distinct, time-sensitive information submissions tied to different triggers: an initial submission after the incident occurs, and subsequent updates after significant changes in circumstances. The initial obligation is to submit information about the CTP operational incident as soon as practicable after the occurrence of the incident, limited to what it is aware of at the time it submits that information. [#TGT:69933824d660799f] Separately, once an initial report has been made and any intermediate incident report has already been submitted, the critical third party must provide additional information as soon as practicable after any significant change from what was previously described, including when the CTP operational incident is resolved, again limited to what it is aware of at the relevant time. [#SRC:de95dc63af31c5be] This later obligation is not just to submit more detail in the abstract; it is specifically to provide information further to what has already been disclosed, and it must be provided to both the regulators and the affected firms. [#SRC:de95dc63af31c5be] Taken together, the compliance approach is: submit incident information promptly after occurrence, then continue to update promptly when circumstances materially change (including resolution), ensuring the updates go to regulators and affected firms. [#TGT:69933824d660799f] [#SRC:de95dc63af31c5be]","A critical third party must, as soon as is practicable after any significant change in circumstances from that described in the initial report submitted under 8.1 and any intermediate incident report already submitted under this rule (including the CTP operational incident being resolved) and in so far as it is aware at the relevant time, provide the regulators and the affected firms with information further to that already disclosed in relation to the CTP operational incident , including but not limited to:","A critical third party must, as soon as is practicable after the occurrence of a CTP operational incident and in so far as it is aware at the time of submission, submit the following information about the CTP operational incident :",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,de95dc63af31c5be,69933824d660799f,,,de95dc63af31c5be,69933824d660799f,,,,,HV0106,a9cf7943a6f83fe5,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

872b3037ff11f7d2,"When a firm is planning a major migration programme and has only shortlisted potential providers (so a final provider has not yet been selected), what should it do about notifying the regulator, and what documentation requirement still applies to the outsourcing arrangement once it proceeds?","A firm planning a major migration programme may consider notifying before it has chosen the final provider, particularly where it is still selecting from a shortlist, because early notification can be appropriate in those circumstances. [#SRC:f9f533f94194f92e] Separately, when the outsourcing arrangement is put in place, the arrangement must be documented in a written agreement, and the firm should review that written agreement to confirm it meets the firm’s regulatory obligations and risk management expectations. [#TGT:9752e97c411082aa] [#SRC:f9f533f94194f92e] In practice, this means the firm can (i) make an earlier notification during provider selection for a major migration programme, and then (ii) ensure the eventual outsourcing is fully captured in a written agreement that is checked against regulatory and risk-management expectations before relying on it operationally. [#SRC:f9f533f94194f92e] [#TGT:9752e97c411082aa]","reviewing the written agreement to ensure it complies with their regulatory obligations and risk management expectations (see Chapter 6 ). In some circumstances, it might be appropriate to make a notification before a final provider has been selected. An example of this is if a firm is planning a major migration programme and is still trying to select a provider from a shortlist.","In line with Article 31(3) of MODR (banks) and Conditions Governing Business 7.5(3) (insurers), all outsourcing arrangements must be set out in a written agreement.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,f9f533f94194f92e,9752e97c411082aa,,,f9f533f94194f92e,9752e97c411082aa,,,,,HV0107,872b3037ff11f7d2,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

fe6cadb25ae512e8,"If a firm is planning to issue an item on the same terms as a basic own funds item issued in the last 12 months (with only the issue date, maturity date, amount, currency, and interest rate allowed to differ), and it already sent the first notification but then wants to change what it submitted before the item is issued, what does it need to do and how quickly?","If the planned item is being issued on identical terms to one or more items that were included in the basic own funds forming the own funds eligible for the group SCR and were issued by the undertaking in the group within the previous 12 months, then “identical terms” allows differences only for the issue date, maturity date, amount of the issuance, currency of the issuance, and the rate of interest payable by the issuer. [#SRC:7114cf075695c1d8] Once the firm has made the initial notification for the item, if it then proposes (before the item is issued) to change any of the information it previously submitted, it must send another written notification covering that change. [#TGT:b15834f057327c97] The timing requirement is immediate in the sense that the further written notification must be provided without delay, and it applies specifically in the window after the initial notification but prior to issuance. [#TGT:b15834f057327c97] This means the firm should not wait until issuance to correct or update details; any proposed change to the previously submitted information—whether it relates to the “identical terms” description or other submitted details—must be re-notified promptly in writing before the item is issued. [#SRC:7114cf075695c1d8] [#TGT:b15834f057327c97]","(3) any item which is to be issued on identical terms to one or more items included in the basic own funds forming the own funds eligible for the group SCR issued by the undertaking in the group within the previous 12 months and notified to the PRA in accordance with 6.2 , excluding (1) the issue date, (2) the maturity date, (3) the amount of the issuance, (4) the currency of the issuance, and (5) the rate of interest payable by the issuer.","If after an initial notification under 6.2 , but prior to an item’s issuance, a firm proposes to change the information previously submitted, it must provide a further written notification of that change without delay.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,7114cf075695c1d8,b15834f057327c97,,,7114cf075695c1d8,b15834f057327c97,,,,,HV0108,fe6cadb25ae512e8,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

49917f7c055c5bc0,"When the PRA assesses whether minimum requirements applied to an entity established outside the United Kingdom exceed that entity’s share of consolidated group requirements for the same risk type, how should the PRA treat a situation where a PRA authorised firm calculates consolidated capital using an IRB model but an overseas subsidiary must use a standardised approach for the same credit risk portfolio, resulting in higher individual or sub-consolidated requirements?","In that scenario, the PRA’s assessment focuses on whether, for the relevant risk type, the minimum requirements applied to the non-UK entity on an individual or sub-consolidated basis exceed the entity’s share of the consolidated group requirements for the same risk. [#SRC:ef9de1e6e4142317] However, where the consolidated group requirement is calculated using an IRB model for a portfolio of credit risk exposures, and the overseas subsidiary must instead apply a standardised approach for the same portfolio—leading to higher requirements at the subsidiary level—the PRA would not count that difference when assessing group risk. [#TGT:723e2d0bc5ddaf68] This treatment aligns with the PRA’s general approach of not taking into account requirements that are attributable to risks already mitigated through the risk-based capital framework or by other means, and not taking into account requirements that net off in consolidation (such as intragroup risks and offsetting positions). [#SRC:ef9de1e6e4142317] Accordingly, even though the subsidiary’s local calculation method produces higher requirements for the same credit risk portfolio, that uplift is excluded from the PRA’s group-risk assessment of the excess over the subsidiary’s share of consolidated requirements. [#TGT:723e2d0bc5ddaf68]","the extent to which, for any given risk type, the minimum requirements applied to an entity established outside the United Kingdom, on an individual or sub-consolidated basis, exceed the entity’s share 19 of the consolidated group requirements for the same risk. When making this assessment, the PRA would not generally take into account requirements that are attributable to risks that: (i) are already mitigated through the risk based capital framework 20 or by other means; 21 or (ii) net off in consolidation (for example, intragroup risks and offsetting positions); and","20. For example, a PRA authorised firm may have permission to use an IRB model to calculate consolidated capital requirements in respect of a portfolio of credit risk exposures. If its overseas subsidiary is required to use a standardised approach for the same portfolio of credit risk exposures (on an individual or sub-consolidated basis), and as a result, it is subject to higher requirements in respect of that portfolio, the PRA would not take the difference into account in its assessment of group risk.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,ef9de1e6e4142317,723e2d0bc5ddaf68,,,ef9de1e6e4142317,723e2d0bc5ddaf68,,,,,HV0109,49917f7c055c5bc0,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

ce23ef288fcc6cf4,"When designing a firm’s governance arrangements for liquidity risk, what must the insurer’s monitoring and reporting system deliver to decision-makers and relevant functions, and how must that be integrated into the firm-wide governance expectation for cooperation, internal reporting, and communication at all relevant levels?","An insurer should structure its liquidity risk monitoring and reporting so that it reliably supports decision-making while also fitting within a governance framework that enables effective cooperation and information flow across the firm. The insurer is expected to have an effective system for monitoring and reporting liquidity risk that produces reports which are clear, concise, timely, and accurate for the relevant functions within the insurer, and the fast-moving nature of liquidity risk should be reflected in how the reporting system operates (for example, in its responsiveness and timeliness). [#SRC:c6c19d84cebb7ce5] In parallel, the firm’s system of governance must establish, implement, and maintain effective cooperation, internal reporting, and communication of information at all relevant levels of the firm, so liquidity risk reporting should be embedded in those firm-wide channels rather than operating in isolation. [#TGT:ecd277e44d328d29] Taken together, this means the insurer must (i) put in place reporting processes and procedures that ensure necessary information is available to decision-makers, (ii) deliver liquidity risk reports meeting the stated quality characteristics to relevant internal functions, and (iii) ensure those reports and related information are communicated through governance arrangements that promote cooperation and internal reporting across all relevant levels. [#SRC:c6c19d84cebb7ce5] [#TGT:ecd277e44d328d29]","Under Conditions Governing Business 2A.1(8) and Non-Solvency II Firms – Governance 7.1 , an insurer must establish systems for the management of risk. Conditions Governing Business 3.1(1A)(d) and Non-Solvency II Firms – Governance 2.5 and 3.2 require the establishment of reporting processes and procedures to ensure that the necessary information is available to decision-makers. With these obligations in mind, the PRA expects an insurer to have an effective system of monitoring and reporting liquidity risk which provides clear, concise, timely and accurate liquidity risk reports to relevant functions within the insurer. Liquidity risks are often fast moving, a characteristic which is expected be reflected in an insurer’s reporting system. Design of metrics and reporting is set out in more detail in Chapter 6 .","(1) the system of governance referred to at paragraph 2.2(1) establishes, implements and maintains effective cooperation, internal reporting and communication of information at all relevant levels of the firm ;",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,c6c19d84cebb7ce5,ecd277e44d328d29,,,c6c19d84cebb7ce5,ecd277e44d328d29,,,,,HV0110,ce23ef288fcc6cf4,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

0d935037aaab1bb6,"When calculating the NPL ratio as a ratio of non-performing loans to total loans, what specific reported fields may be used to determine the non-performing loans figure, and how does that figure fit into the overall ratio calculation?","To compute the NPL ratio, you must express non-performing loans as the numerator and total loans as the denominator, because the ratio is defined as non-performing loans divided by total loans. [#SRC:100c416be2d4ca28] For the numerator, the non-performing loans amount may be determined using the sum of specified reported fields, depending on the reporting framework used. [#TGT:1674bc5320648995] In particular, non-performing loans can be calculated as the sum of the fields firms are required to report in form FSA015 (11G, 11Q, 20B, 20D, 23B, 23D, 26B, 26D, 31B, 31C). [#TGT:1674bc5320648995] Alternatively, the non-performing loans figure may be taken from FINREP as row 330, column 060 of F18.00, or from FINREP F7.00 using the combination of row 0190 columns 060, 070, 080 and 090. [#TGT:1674bc5320648995] Once the non-performing loans numerator is determined using one of these reporting-based definitions, it is then divided by total loans to produce the NPL ratio. [#SRC:100c416be2d4ca28]",NPL ratio will be calculated as the ratio of non-performing loans 4 to total loans. 5,"4. Defined as the sum of the following fields as firms are required to report in form FSA015: 11G, 11Q, 20B, 20D, 23B, 23D, 26B, 26D, 31B, 31C; or row 330, column 060 of F18.00 (FINREP); or row 0190 column 060, row 0190 column 070, row 0190 column 080 and row 0190 column 090 of F7.00 (FINREP).",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,100c416be2d4ca28,1674bc5320648995,,,100c416be2d4ca28,1674bc5320648995,,,,,HV0111,0d935037aaab1bb6,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

9872519f71bdf7c6,"Where a claim is treated as suspended and the FSCS has decided not to pursue recoveries, how is the point at which the claim is treated as paid determined if the compensation recipient asks in writing to pursue recoveries themselves and seeks an assignment of rights back from the FSCS?","If the FSCS has decided not to pursue recoveries and the compensation recipient asks in writing to pursue them, the FSCS is required to assign the relevant rights back to the compensation recipient. [#TGT:4df8d3ca566204fc] In that situation, the claim is treated as paid only when (and only to the extent that) recoveries are actually made from the credit institution or a third party in respect of the eligible deposit, and those recoveries may be made either by the FSCS or by the person to whom rights have been assigned back (i.e., the depositor/compensation recipient once the assignment occurs). [#SRC:09c735f8e9adc351] Practically, this means the written request and resulting assignment do not, by themselves, cause the suspended claim to be treated as paid; payment treatment is tied to the timing and amount of recoveries achieved after the assignment (or by the FSCS if it makes recoveries). [#SRC:09c735f8e9adc351] The linkage is that the FSCS’s obligation to assign rights back upon a written request applies specifically when it has chosen not to pursue recoveries, and once rights are assigned back, recoveries made by the compensation recipient are the recoveries that determine when and to what extent the claim is deemed paid. [#TGT:4df8d3ca566204fc] [#SRC:09c735f8e9adc351]",Any claim of B against the depositor that is suspended in accordance with 28.2A is only deemed to have been paid for the purposes of regulation 24(1)(b) of the Electronic Money Regulations or regulation 23(14)(b) of the Payment Services Regulations when (and to the extent) the FSCS (or the depositor where the FSCS assigns rights back to the depositor in accordance with 29.2 ) has made recoveries from the credit institution or any third party in respect of the eligible deposit .,"If the FSCS decides not to pursue such recoveries and a compensation recipient wishes to pursue those recoveries and so requests in writing, the FSCS must comply with that request and assign the rights back to the compensation recipient .",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,09c735f8e9adc351,4df8d3ca566204fc,,,09c735f8e9adc351,4df8d3ca566204fc,,,,,HV0112,9872519f71bdf7c6,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

db00d79d2582fc39,"When the PRA is considering using its power to direct a society to transfer all its engagements to one or more other societies (including where negotiations are already under way), how does the PRA determine whether the assessment should focus on whether members (or a proportion of them) would be unreasonably prejudiced, and how does that modified approach interact with the PRA’s ability to require approval by board resolution rather than a member vote?","Where the PRA is acting in circumstances that trigger the modified merger procedure, it may apply a special, consolidated test focused on whether members (or a proportion of them) would be unreasonably prejudiced by the transfer, rather than applying the usual first and second tests separately. [#SRC:2aacec38e1160f5f] Whether that special test applies is not automatic; it is a matter for the PRA’s judgement based on any representations it receives and its own enquiries into the particular case. [#SRC:2aacec38e1160f5f] In parallel, the PRA has a power—where it considers it expedient to protect the investments of shareholders or depositors—to direct a society to transfer all its engagements to one or more other societies within a specified period, and the statutory framework described also contemplates a modified merger procedure in consequence. [#TGT:0aeb091942915c7e] In that directed-transfer context (or where the PRA would have directed a transfer but negotiations were already under way), the PRA may additionally direct that the transferor society’s approval can be given by board resolution rather than by a member Merger Resolution. [#TGT:0aeb091942915c7e] Consistently with this, when the PRA considers the further criterion it must assess, it takes account of the fact that the procedure has been modified. [#SRC:2aacec38e1160f5f]","As is noted in paragraph 3.193 , the First and Second Criteria are replaced, in those circumstances, by a single criterion as to whether the members or a proportion of them would be unreasonably prejudiced by the transfer. Whether this special criterion applies will be a matter of judgement for the PRA to make in the light of any representations made to it and its own enquiries in respect of the particular case. It follows also that, in considering the Third Criterion , the PRA will take account of the modified procedure.","This section describes the PRA’s powers to direct a society to transfer all its engagements to one or more other societies and/or to proceed by board resolution, and the modified merger procedure consequently prescribed by the 1986 Act. Section 42B of the 1986 Act provides that, if the PRA considers it expedient to do so to protect the investments of shareholders or depositors, it may direct a society, among other things, to transfer all its engagements to one or more other societies within a specified period (subsection (1)(a)). In such a case, or where the PRA would have directed a transfer of engagements, but for the fact that negotiations were already under way, the PRA may also direct that the approval of the transfer of engagements by the transferor society may be by board resolution rather than by Merger Resolution.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,2aacec38e1160f5f,0aeb091942915c7e,,,2aacec38e1160f5f,0aeb091942915c7e,,,,,HV0113,db00d79d2582fc39,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

fd828d396136ee70,"For a firm that has a matching adjustment permission and chooses to use the EVT when preparing the required attestation for each relevant portfolio of assets as a whole, what approach must it take to the EVT’s principles and assumptions, including any minimum parameters and treatment of retained risks?","A firm with a matching adjustment permission must submit an attestation to the PRA for each relevant portfolio of assets as a whole, and that attestation must be provided at the required time, by the required person, and in the required form. [#TGT:e4cd8736edad498d] If, in preparing that required attestation, the firm chooses to use the EVT for attestation purposes, the PRA expects the firm to engage with the principles that underpin the EVT rather than applying it mechanically. [#SRC:bac9c4bd1480db48] In doing so, the firm should use its own assumptions that it judges appropriate for attesting that the matching adjustment can be earned with a high degree of confidence from the assets held in the relevant portfolio. [#SRC:bac9c4bd1480db48] Those assumptions should not be set below the PRA’s published minimum parameters where such parameters apply. [#SRC:bac9c4bd1480db48] The firm should also give additional consideration to any retained risks other than the NNEG that are not assessed by the EVT, so that the attestation appropriately reflects risks not captured by the EVT approach. [#SRC:bac9c4bd1480db48]","Where a firm chooses to use the EVT for attestation purposes, the PRA expects it to engage with the principles underlying the EVT and use its own assumptions that are judged to be appropriate when attesting that the MA can be earned with a high degree of confidence from the assets held in the relevant portfolio of assets ( Matching Adjustment 9.1(1)(b) ). These assumptions should not fall below the PRA’s published minimum parameters where applicable, with additional consideration given to any retained risks other than the NNEG that are not assessed by the EVT.",A firm with a matching adjustment permission must provide to the PRA the attestation set out at (1) at the time set out in (2) by a person in (3) in the form set out in 12.1 in respect of each relevant portfolio of assets as a whole held by the firm .,DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,bac9c4bd1480db48,e4cd8736edad498d,,,bac9c4bd1480db48,e4cd8736edad498d,,,,,HV0114,fd828d396136ee70,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

99f3b1ddfcaccec1,"When the PRA receives an MA application, what decision timeframe should a firm plan for, and how does that expectation change depending on whether the firm provides sufficient-quality evidence with limited follow-up versus insufficient evidence requiring material iterative dialogue (including where a streamlined approach is suitable)?","A firm should plan on the PRA aiming to decide an MA application within six months of receiving it, but should also expect that the actual time to decision depends on the quality and completeness of the evidence provided and the extent of follow-up engagement needed. [#SRC:e05922df7b656058] The PRA’s baseline expectation is to provide its decision no later than six months from receipt of the firm’s application. [#SRC:e05922df7b656058] This six-month expectation is framed on the assumption that the firm supplies evidence of sufficient quality for the PRA to decide and that requests for additional information or clarification are limited. [#TGT:21bff8d22b1aaa7c] If those assumptions are met, the PRA expects to determine the outcome within six months from the date of receipt. [#TGT:21bff8d22b1aaa7c] If a streamlined approach is considered suitable, the PRA would expect to reach a decision more quickly than the six-month outer expectation. [#SRC:e05922df7b656058] Conversely, where insufficient evidence is provided and/or there is a need for material iterative dialogue between the PRA and the firm, the time needed for the PRA to reach a decision is likely to be extended beyond the standard expectation. [#TGT:21bff8d22b1aaa7c]","The PRA is committed to assessing and providing decisions on all MA applications as quickly as possible, and expects to give its decision no later than six months from its receipt of a firm’s application (subject to the points made in paragraph 2.29 of this SoP). If a streamlined approach is considered suitable, then the PRA would expect to reach a decision more quickly.","Assuming that the firm has provided a sufficient quality of evidence to allow the PRA to make a decision, and that the need for additional information and/or clarification has been limited, the PRA expects to determine the outcome of an application no later than six months from the date of receipt. Where insufficient evidence is provided and/or there is need for material iterative dialogue between the PRA and the firm, this is likely to extend the time needed for the PRA to reach a decision.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,e05922df7b656058,21bff8d22b1aaa7c,,,e05922df7b656058,21bff8d22b1aaa7c,,,,,HV0115,99f3b1ddfcaccec1,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

a0927dbe81380a29,"When deciding whether to give confirmation for an amalgamation or transfer, how should the PRA treat a failure to meet a requirement in the Friendly Societies Act 1992 or the rules of a participating society, and in what circumstances can the PRA modify requirements based on an application by members?","The PRA must withhold confirmation if it concludes that a relevant requirement in the Friendly Societies Act 1992 or in the rules of any participating society has not been met, because that type of non-fulfilment is a stated ground on which confirmation must not be given. [#SRC:c0235e996b557c4a] However, the PRA is not limited to a binary “met/not met” assessment: it can modify some requirements and can direct that certain failures may be disregarded, which can affect whether a particular non-compliance remains a bar to confirmation. [#SRC:c0235e996b557c4a] Separately, and as a concrete route to modification, the PRA has discretion to modify some requirements for a transfer of engagements from a friendly society where a specified number of the society’s members apply and the PRA is satisfied that making the modification is expedient in the interests of the society’s members or potential members. [#TGT:479c243b93b94186] In practice, this means that if a requirement shortfall would otherwise prevent confirmation, the PRA can only move away from that outcome where it uses its modification power (including on a qualifying member application) so that the relevant requirement is adjusted and/or the failure is treated as one that may be disregarded. [#SRC:c0235e996b557c4a][#TGT:479c243b93b94186]","(1) confirmation must not be given if the PRA considers that: (a) there is a substantial risk that the successor society or transferee will be lawfully unable to carry out the engagements to be transferred to it. For the purposes of this condition, the PRA may have regard to the requirements of any country outside of the UK which appear to be relevant; (b) information material to the members’ decision about the amalgamation or transfer was not made available to all the members eligible to vote; (c) the vote on any resolution approving the amalgamation or transfer does not represent the views of the members eligible to vote; or (d) some relevant requirement of the Friendly Societies Act 1992 or the rules of any of the participating societies was not fulfilled (but it can modify some requirements and direct that certain failures may be disregarded, see 4.13 above and 4.28 below);","The PRA has discretion under section 89 of the Friendly Societies Act 1992 to modify some of the requirements for a transfer of engagements from a friendly society, on the application of a specified number of its members, if it is satisfied that it is expedient to do so in the interests of its members or potential members.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,c0235e996b557c4a,479c243b93b94186,,,c0235e996b557c4a,479c243b93b94186,,,,,HV0116,a0927dbe81380a29,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

433f59e6d3bf883b,"If a transfer plan would raise pay for directors or other officers because of the transfer, what vote has to be held and who votes on it, and what must be included in the Transfer Statement so the PRA can decide on the society’s confirmation application?","When the transfer terms include a pay increase for directors or other officers because of the transfer, the society must put an ordinary resolution about that pay increase to a meeting of the society. [#SRC:7b4a2555806fbf1b] That ordinary resolution is decided by a simple majority of the members who are entitled to vote and who do vote, with shareholding and borrowing members voting together. [#SRC:7b4a2555806fbf1b] The meeting for this ordinary resolution does not have to be the same meeting that considers the Transfer Resolutions. [#TGT:59f0c65404b632d5] Also, even though the ordinary resolution must be put to a meeting, it does not need to be approved to make the pay increase effective, because the increase is authorised through the overall approval of the transfer and its terms when the Transfer Resolutions pass. [#TGT:59f0c65404b632d5] Separately, the proposed pay increase must be explained in the Transfer Statement, and the PRA must be satisfied (when reviewing the society’s application for confirmation of the transfer) that the ordinary resolution was in fact put before a meeting of the society. [#TGT:59f0c65404b632d5] This gives members a distinct chance to comment on pay changes apart from the main transfer decision. [#SRC:7b4a2555806fbf1b]","As is described in paragraphs 4.82 and 4.83 , if the terms of a transfer include provision for increased emoluments of directors or other officers in consequence of the transfer, an ordinary resolution approving any such provision must be put before a meeting of the society. An ordinary resolution is passed by a simple majority of members (both shareholding and borrowing members voting together) qualified to vote and voting. However, it is not required that the resolution must be put to the same meeting as the Transfer Resolutions, neither is approval of the ordinary resolution required to authorise such increased emoluments which, as terms of the transfer, are authorised by the passage of the Transfer Resolutions. The purpose of Section 99A of the 1986 Act is to give the members an opportunity to express their views on these matters separately from their decision on whether or not to approve the transfer and its terms.","Any such increase in emoluments is required by Section 99A(2) of the 1986 Act to be put before a meeting of the society in an ordinary resolution approving such provision. However, although such an ordinary resolution must be put to a meeting, it is not required to be passed in order to authorise such increases which will be authorised by the general approval of the transfer and its terms provided by the passage of the Transfer Resolutions. Neither is it required that the ordinary resolution be put before the meeting which is to consider the Transfer Resolutions. However, as is explained below, any proposed increase in emoluments will have to be explained in the Transfer Statement, and the PRA will have to be satisfied that the requisite ordinary resolution was put before a meeting of the society when it considers a society’s application for confirmation of a transfer.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,7b4a2555806fbf1b,59f0c65404b632d5,,,7b4a2555806fbf1b,59f0c65404b632d5,,,,,HV0117,433f59e6d3bf883b,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

7e5254a08f4c0af7,"If a firm changes its MA portfolio without obtaining approval from the PRA to vary its MA permission, what are the consequences for its ability to apply a matching adjustment when calculating the best estimate, and what remediation timeline applies if the changes cause the MA eligibility conditions to be breached?","A firm may only apply a matching adjustment when calculating the best estimate of its insurance or reinsurance obligations if it has a matching adjustment permission; without that permission it must not apply the adjustment to the relevant risk-free interest rate term structure. [#TGT:78efaa111a0c4a1d] Separately, if the firm makes changes to its MA portfolio without obtaining PRA approval to vary its MA permission (and those changes are outside the scope of what is contemplated in the referenced context), that conduct is treated as a breach for which the PRA would consider using its supervisory powers. [#SRC:4b18983e4bca375c] In addition, where the changes to the MA portfolio lead to a breach of the MA eligibility conditions, the firm must restore compliance with the relevant condition(s) within two months to avoid a reduction to the matching adjustment. [#SRC:4b18983e4bca375c] Taken together, the firm should ensure it both holds the required permission before applying the matching adjustment in best-estimate calculations and, if portfolio changes have caused eligibility non-compliance, completes remediation within the two-month window to prevent a reduction. [#TGT:78efaa111a0c4a1d] [#SRC:4b18983e4bca375c]","If a firm makes changes to its MA portfolio without obtaining approval from the PRA to vary its MA permission, and if these changes are outside the scope of what is contemplated in paragraph 9.1A above, this would constitute a breach of Matching Adjustment 2.1 , in respect of which the PRA would consider exercising its supervisory powers. If changes made to the MA portfolio result in a breach of the MA eligibility conditions, then the firm will need to restore compliance with the relevant condition(s) within two months in order to avoid a reduction to the MA.",A firm must not apply a matching adjustment to the relevant risk-free interest rate term structure to calculate the best estimate of its insurance or reinsurance obligations unless it has a matching adjustment permission .,DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,4b18983e4bca375c,78efaa111a0c4a1d,,,4b18983e4bca375c,78efaa111a0c4a1d,,,,,HV0118,7e5254a08f4c0af7,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

5608c374a74adc0e,"When a firm is required to have written policies and procedures covering risk management, internal control, internal audit and (where relevant) outsourcing, what specific content must those policies include and how must that content align with the firm’s broader direction?","A firm that is required to establish, implement and maintain written policies and adequate procedures for risk management, internal control, internal audit and, where relevant, outsourcing must ensure those written policies are drafted with sufficient operational detail and strategic alignment. Specifically, the firm must have written policies and adequate procedures in place for at least those functions (and outsourcing where relevant), and must keep them established, implemented, and maintained as written documentation. [#TGT:223fc6e5205a9c72] In addition, the firm must ensure its policies in these areas clearly describe (i) who is responsible for what, (ii) the objectives of the arrangements, (iii) the processes to be followed, and (iv) the reporting procedures that will be applied. [#SRC:d73247674d265abb] Finally, the responsibilities, objectives, processes, and reporting procedures set out in those policies must be consistent with the firm’s overall business strategy, so the written framework for these control functions does not conflict with how the firm intends to operate and manage its business. [#SRC:d73247674d265abb]","A firm must ensure that its policies on risk-management, internal control, internal audit and, where relevant, outsourcing referred to in 2.4(1) clearly set out the relevant responsibilities, objectives, processes and reporting procedures to be applied, all of which must be consistent with the firm’s overall business strategy.","(1) establish, implement and maintain written policies and adequate procedures in relation to at least risk management, internal control, internal audit and, where relevant, outsourcing ;",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,d73247674d265abb,223fc6e5205a9c72,,,d73247674d265abb,223fc6e5205a9c72,,,,,HV0119,5608c374a74adc0e,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

cc08595658c186fc,"When a firm rates tenants and uses those ratings to derive a probability of non-rent payment, what expectation applies to how intuitive that transformation should be, and how should the firm treat the relationship between the resulting PD and actual non-payment—particularly when considering divergence between observed default rates and PD across different economic conditions in the mid-corporate space?","The firm should ensure that converting tenant ratings into a probability of non-rent payment is done in a way that is intuitive, rather than opaque or hard to interpret. [#SRC:091fac39c7e6e49b] At the same time, even if tenants are rated by the firm, the firm should not assume the resulting PD is typically a direct read-across to the probability of non-payment, because factors such as model philosophy can break that one-to-one mapping. [#TGT:43ecedb5d0451d08] In practice, this means the firm needs to explicitly address and articulate what divergence it expects between observed default rates and PD, and how that divergence may vary under different economic conditions, with particular attention to the mid-corporate space where firms often struggle with this definition. [#TGT:43ecedb5d0451d08] The compliance outcome is a coherent approach where (i) the rating-to-non-payment-probability transformation remains intuitive to users and reviewers, and (ii) the firm documents and manages the anticipated gap between PD outputs and observed non-payment/default experience rather than treating PD as a direct proxy for non-payment. [#SRC:091fac39c7e6e49b] [#TGT:43ecedb5d0451d08]",(b) the transformation of ratings into non-rent payment probability is intuitive; 12,"12. Even where tenants are rated by the firm the PD will not usually represent a direct read across to probability of non-payment due to, for example, model philosophy issues. Addressing this is likely to be a key area since many firms struggle with defining what divergence is expected between observed default rate and PD in different economic conditions in the mid-corporate space.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,091fac39c7e6e49b,43ecedb5d0451d08,,,091fac39c7e6e49b,43ecedb5d0451d08,,,,,HV0120,cc08595658c186fc,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

5291250dbbe646b9,"When coordinating regulatory functions for an RFTS, how should responsibility be allocated between the PRA and the FCA for leading the process and issuing the certificate of financial resources to the court, including the exception where the transferee is an FCA solo regulated entity, and how is this coordination framework documented?","For an RFTS, the PRA is the default lead regulator for the overall process, and it is also the regulator responsible for specific regulatory functions connected with RFTS applications, including providing certificates under FSMA. [#TGT:39a1985ef6854457] However, there is a defined exception for the certificate of financial resources: where the transferee is an FCA solo regulated entity, the FCA (not the PRA) issues that certificate to the court. [#TGT:39a1985ef6854457] This allocation of responsibilities sits within a broader statutory context in which FSMA prescribes functions for both the PRA and the FCA in relation to RFTS, and the two regulators are expected to coordinate how they exercise those functions where there is common regulatory interest. [#SRC:5f2897ab41776611] The coordination framework is documented through a Memorandum of Understanding maintained by the PRA and the FCA, which describes each regulator’s role in exercising its FSMA functions on matters of common regulatory interest and explains how they intend to ensure those functions are exercised in a coordinated way. [#SRC:5f2897ab41776611]","FSMA 5 also prescribes certain statutory functions in relation to RFTS for both the PRA and FCA. In accordance with FSMA, the PRA and the FCA maintain a Memorandum of Understanding 6 which describes each regulator’s role in relation to the exercise of its functions under FSMA relating to matters of common regulatory interest and how each regulator intends to ensure the co-ordinated exercise of such functions.","The PRA will lead the process for the RFTS. As described above, the PRA will also be responsible for specific regulatory functions connected with RFTS applications including the provision of certificates under section 111 of FSMA. The only exception to this is when the transferee is an FCA solo regulated entity. In this instance, the FCA will issue the certificate of financial resources to the court.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,5f2897ab41776611,39a1985ef6854457,,,5f2897ab41776611,39a1985ef6854457,,,,,HV0121,5291250dbbe646b9,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

ba2795f1c51b082e,"For a firm calculating the required margin of solvency for classes III and VII, how must the firm adjust that required margin when it covers a death risk, including where the required margin would otherwise be zero?","When a firm is determining the required margin of solvency for classes III and VII, it must use the calculation framework specified for those classes and then apply an additional adjustment if it covers a death risk. [#SRC:a3e39e9b0ab41484] Specifically, the required margin of solvency for classes III and VII must be calculated in accordance with the set of calculations referenced for those classes. [#SRC:a3e39e9b0ab41484] If the firm covers a death risk, it must add an extra amount to the required margin of solvency that it has arrived at under the relevant calculation routes, and this applies even if the required margin of solvency would otherwise be zero. [#TGT:d279a616f589ab73] The added amount is the sum produced by applying the specified calculation, but with the stated exclusions from that calculation applied for this purpose. [#TGT:d279a616f589ab73] In other words, the firm first computes the required margin of solvency for the relevant classes using the referenced class-based methodology, and then, where death risk is covered, increases that result by the separately computed add-on amount (computed using the specified calculation with the noted parts excluded). [#SRC:a3e39e9b0ab41484] [#TGT:d279a616f589ab73]",A firm must calculate the required margin of solvency in respect of classes III and VII in accordance with 3.2 to 3.4 .,"Where a firm covers a death risk, a sum arrived at by applying the calculation in 2.3 (but excluding for these purposes 2.3 (4) and (5)) must be added to the required margin of solvency , including a required margin of solvency of zero, arrived at under any of 3.2 and 3.3 .",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,a3e39e9b0ab41484,d279a616f589ab73,,,a3e39e9b0ab41484,d279a616f589ab73,,,,,HV0122,ba2795f1c51b082e,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

d6c5ac2d4ee8a8c1,"If the rules have to be applied across the whole group (with any needed changes), what does the firm need to do regularly about its governance system, and what should it do when it finds problems?","If the situation is one where the listed requirements are to be applied at the level of the group (with any necessary changes), the firm should treat the governance expectation as operating across the group rather than only within a single firm entity. [#SRC:bb599b0cccb14552] In that setting, the firm has an ongoing duty to keep its system of governance under review by monitoring it and regularly evaluating whether it is adequate and effective. [#TGT:819ccde69365886c] Where that monitoring and evaluation shows shortcomings, the firm must take appropriate measures to fix or otherwise address those deficiencies. [#TGT:819ccde69365886c] Read together, this means the firm’s regular governance checks and any corrective actions should be performed in a way that fits the group-level application of the requirements (i.e., adjusted as needed for the group context). [#SRC:bb599b0cccb14552] [#TGT:819ccde69365886c]","(1) Where 2.1(1) or 2.1(2) applies, the following requirements apply with any necessary changes at the level of the group : (1a) Conditions Governing Business 1A ; (a) Conditions Governing Business 2.2 to 2.6 ; (a1) Conditions Governing Business 2A.1 to 2A.6 ; (b) Conditions Governing Business 3 ; (b1) Conditions Governing Business 3A ; (c) Conditions Governing Business 4 ; (c1) Conditions Governing Business 4A ; (d) Conditions Governing Business 5 ; (e) Conditions Governing Business 6 ; (f) Conditions Governing Business 7 ; (f1) Conditions Governing Business 11A to 11F ; (g) Fitness and Propriety 2.1 to 2.3 , 4.1 , 4.3 and 4.4 ; (h) Allocation of Responsibilities 4 ; and (i) Key Function Holder – Notifications 2 to 6 , in accordance with 17.4 .","A firm must monitor, and on a regular basis evaluate, the adequacy and effectiveness of its system of governance and take appropriate measures to address any deficiencies.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,bb599b0cccb14552,819ccde69365886c,,,bb599b0cccb14552,819ccde69365886c,,,,,HV0123,d6c5ac2d4ee8a8c1,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

c067ff1441e73431,"When setting a firm’s capital stack, how should the PRA buffer relate to the firm’s total capital requirement and the combined buffer, and what specific buffer components must be included when calculating the combined buffer (including any scope limitation for particular firms)?","A firm’s capital stack should be constructed so that the PRA buffer (Pillar 2B) sits on top of, and is held in addition to, both the firm’s total capital requirement and the combined buffer; its purpose is to absorb losses under a severe stress scenario while being set in a way that avoids duplicating what is already covered by the combined buffers. [#SRC:37bcd95fb7b21224] In this framework, the PRA buffer, the combined buffer, and the total capital requirement together form the PRA’s overall capital framework (i.e., the capital stack is the sum of these layers). [#SRC:37bcd95fb7b21224] To calculate the combined buffer layer that the PRA buffer must avoid duplicating, the combined buffer must include the Capital Conservation Buffer, the Countercyclical Buffer, and the buffer for global systemically important institutions. [#TGT:9c1fa36fe39c19a7] In addition, for ring-fenced banks and the largest building societies, the combined buffer also includes the other systemically important institutions buffer (O-SII buffer), meaning this component applies only within that stated firm scope. [#TGT:9c1fa36fe39c19a7]","The PRA buffer (also referred to as Pillar 2B) is an amount of capital firms should maintain in addition to their total capital requirement 32 (TCR) and the combined buffer. The PRA buffer absorbs losses that may arise under a severe stress scenario, while avoiding duplication with the combined buffers. Together the PRA buffer, the combined buffer 33 and the TCR make up the PRA’s capital framework as illustrated by the capital stack in Figure 2.","33. The combined buffer comprises the Capital Conservation Buffer (CCoB), the Countercyclical Buffer (CCyB), the buffer for global systemically important institutions (G-SIIs) and (for ring-fenced banks and the largest building societies) the other systemically important institutions buffer (O-SII buffer).",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,37bcd95fb7b21224,9c1fa36fe39c19a7,,,37bcd95fb7b21224,9c1fa36fe39c19a7,,,,,HV0124,c067ff1441e73431,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

ca019e83ad724f49,"When assessing whether a firm’s culture supports prudent management, what specific responsibilities does the board have, what behaviours are expected from individuals across the firm, and what indicators will the PRA look for to be satisfied that risk management and control functions have real influence—particularly in relation to challenging orthodoxies, understanding when viability is at risk, and taking timely action on risks?","A firm should be able to demonstrate a culture that supports prudent management, with clear accountability at both board and individual levels, and with risk management and control functions having genuine influence in decision-making. [#SRC:41637720a107d8eb] The board is expected to take responsibility for establishing, embedding, and maintaining the firm’s culture, rather than treating culture as an informal or delegated matter. [#TGT:6a3529e5c660df25] Individuals at all levels are expected to take responsibility for acting in a way that is consistent with the firm’s safety and soundness, and the firm’s remuneration and incentives should reinforce careful and prudent management. [#TGT:6a3529e5c660df25] In evaluating whether the culture is effective (without prescribing a single “right culture”), the PRA will look for evidence that boards and management understand the circumstances in which the firm’s viability would be in question, that accepted orthodoxies are actively challenged, and that risks are addressed on a timely basis. [#SRC:41637720a107d8eb] The PRA also wants to be satisfied that designated risk management and control functions carry real weight within the firm, which should align with the board-led cultural framework and individual responsibility expectations described above. [#SRC:41637720a107d8eb] [#TGT:6a3529e5c660df25]","The PRA expects firms to have a culture that supports their prudent management. The PRA does not have any ‘right culture’ in mind, rather it focuses on whether boards and management clearly understand the circumstances in which the firm’s viability would be under question, whether accepted orthodoxies are challenged, and whether action is taken to address risks on a timely basis. The PRA wants to be satisfied in particular that designated risk management and control functions carry real weight within firms 5 .","The PRA also expects that individuals, whatever their position in the firm, should take responsibility for acting in a manner consistent with its safety and soundness; that remuneration and incentive structures should reward careful and prudent management; that firms and individuals should deal with the PRA (and other regulators as appropriate) in an open and co-operative manner as set out in the PRA’s Fundamental Rules; and that the board takes responsibility for establishing, embedding and maintaining a firm’s culture 6 . The PRA seeks to address serious failings in the culture of firms as part of its approach to supervision.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,41637720a107d8eb,6a3529e5c660df25,,,41637720a107d8eb,6a3529e5c660df25,,,,,HV0125,ca019e83ad724f49,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

d5e836ccef83eaa6,"If members are going to vote on a transfer, but the transferee society wants to approve its promise to take on the transferor society’s commitments through its committee of management (not a special vote), what must members be told before they vote, and what does the PRA look for before it agrees to that committee approach?","Members’ voting on a transfer should only happen after they have been given enough clear information to understand both the transfer terms and how their interests may be affected, and this member-information standard still matters even if the transferee society is asking for a committee of management resolution route for its undertaking. [#SRC:5417d16edd7906ff] The friendly society must ensure that, before votes are cast, members are clearly and fully informed of the terms on which the transfer is to take place and have all information needed to understand the effect on their interests; if information that is material to the decision is not made available to all members eligible to vote, the PRA may decide not to confirm the transfer. [#SRC:5417d16edd7906ff] If the society’s rules allow, delegates can vote, except on an affected members’ resolution. [#SRC:5417d16edd7906ff] On the transferee side, the PRA can allow the undertaking to fulfil the transferor society’s engagements to be approved by a committee of management resolution rather than a special resolution, but it will want comfort that the transfer is in the interests of members of both societies and that it will not mean a change of policy by the transferee society. [#TGT:39ca82df9578b7ff] The PRA is unlikely to allow this unless the transferee is significantly larger than the business being transferred. [#TGT:39ca82df9578b7ff]","Under the Friendly Societies Act 1992, members will normally have the opportunity to vote on a proposed transfer or amalgamation (save for the exceptions set out in 4.12 and 4.13 ). A friendly society has to ensure that, before casting their votes, its members are clearly and fully informed of the terms on which the amalgamation or transfer of engagements is to take place and that they have all the information needed to understand how their interests will be affected. If the society’s rules permit, delegates can vote except on an ‘affected members’ resolution’ under section 86. The PRA may not confirm an amalgamation or a transfer if it considers that information material to the members’ decision was not made available to all the members eligible to vote.","The PRA has discretion under section 86(3)(b) of the Friendly Societies Act 1992 to allow a transferee society to resolve to undertake to fulfil the engagements of a transferor society by resolution of the committee of management, rather than by special resolution. Among the issues that the PRA would wish to be satisfied on before exercising this discretion, are that the transfer will be in the interests of the members of both societies and that the transfer will not mean a change of policy by the transferee society. The PRA is unlikely to exercise this discretion unless the transferee is significantly larger than the business to be transferred.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,5417d16edd7906ff,39ca82df9578b7ff,,,5417d16edd7906ff,39ca82df9578b7ff,,,,,HV0126,d5e836ccef83eaa6,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

6c8f72f9eb49197e,"When a firm is considering operating split desks, what should it do in relation to the PRA, and how might the PRA evaluate and respond to the firm’s proposed changes in light of its expectations about control over UK risks and booking model expectations?","If a firm is considering operating split desks, it should notify the PRA at the point split desks are being considered, reflecting that split desks are viewed as increasing operational risk because the same risk is managed in two locations and therefore requires greater oversight and coordination. [#SRC:4190cc2641fd48ce] In parallel, the firm should be prepared for the PRA to assess whether the proposed changes are compatible with the degree of control the PRA expects the firm to exercise over risks affecting the activities it carries on in the UK, with the extent and manner in which the PRA’s booking model expectations are met being an important factor in that assessment. [#TGT:7ed859d16f359ce8] If the PRA is not satisfied that the proposed changes are appropriate—taking into account the overall degree of integration or separation between the overseas and UK businesses, the controls in place, and other factors—then the PRA may impose conditions or restrictions on what the firm may do. [#TGT:7ed859d16f359ce8] The firm should also ensure that all relevant control functions are satisfied that the split desks are effectively managed, since this structure is not expected to be used extensively. [#SRC:4190cc2641fd48ce]","Split desk considerations: Split desks are associated with higher operational risks since the management of the same risk in two locations, rather than one, increases the extent of oversight and coordination needed. All the relevant control functions should be satisfied that the desks are effectively managed. A firm may need or choose to operate them in some circumstances, but the PRA does not expect this structure to be used extensively. Hence the expectation that firms will notify the PRA when split desks are being considered [ 4.25D - 4.25E above].","The PRA will assess whether the proposed changes are compatible with the degree of control it expects a firm to exercise over risks affecting the activities it carries on in the UK. The extent to which and manner in which the PRA’s booking model expectations (see below) are met will be an important factor in the PRA’s assessment. Where the PRA is not satisfied that the proposed changes are appropriate, taking into account the overall degree of integration or separation between the overseas and UK businesses, the controls in place and other factors set out in this SS, then the PRA may impose conditions or restrictions on what the firm may do. By way of illustration, some specific factors relevant to trading activities that the PRA may consider are:",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,4190cc2641fd48ce,7ed859d16f359ce8,,,4190cc2641fd48ce,7ed859d16f359ce8,,,,,HV0127,6c8f72f9eb49197e,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

083fc14d3daa3e6f,"If there is a transfer event, what is ‘Z B ’ meant to measure in the update, and how does the PRA say a firm can meet the requirement—unless it has a waiver or modification?","For a transfer event, the PRA expects the update to produce ‘Z B ’ as a ratio that captures the dynamic portion of the total TMTP after the transfer as a percentage of the dynamic BEL on the underlying business after the transfer, taking into account that it is subject to any adjustment referenced for that purpose. [#SRC:a2f66dc44340ad31] Firms must make sure the relevant requirement is followed unless they have been granted a waiver or modification under the stated permissions approach. [#TGT:b34bb4d4e11aa3c7] The PRA indicates this can be done in practice by adjusting the value of ‘Z B ’ or by adjusting ‘C 0 ’. [#TGT:b34bb4d4e11aa3c7] Putting these together: when you are working out how the ratio changes because of the transfer event, you use the post-transfer ‘Z B ’ definition for what the ratio represents, and you then ensure adherence by adjusting ‘Z B ’ (or ‘C 0 ’) unless the waiver/modification condition applies. [#SRC:a2f66dc44340ad31] [#TGT:b34bb4d4e11aa3c7]","The PRA expects that the update required by Transitional Measures on Technical Provisions 6 should result in ‘Z B ’, representing the dynamic portion of the total TMTP post transfer as a percentage of the dynamic BEL on the underlying business post transfer subject to any adjustment referred to in 3.7E below. For the purpose of determining how this ratio has changed due to a transfer event:","Firms must ensure that Transitional Measures on Technical Provisions 6.2 is adhered to, unless they have been granted a waiver or modification as set out in 3.3 of the SoP ‘Permissions for transitional measures on technical provisions and risk-free interest rates’. The PRA expects this can be achieved by adjusting the value for ‘Z B ’ or ‘C 0 ’.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,a2f66dc44340ad31,b34bb4d4e11aa3c7,,,a2f66dc44340ad31,b34bb4d4e11aa3c7,,,,,HV0128,083fc14d3daa3e6f,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

6c71c40cbac54bce,"If there is a serious disruption, how should impact tolerances be used to help decisions, and what should the firm have already done (through mapping and testing) to check it can keep important business services within those tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios?","In a disruption, impact tolerances can be used as a decision aid, but they are not the only input: they should be considered alongside other information that is relevant to managing the incident effectively. [#SRC:51a4e8e33523d5d5] Separately, the firm is expected to be able to keep delivering its important business services within impact tolerances even in severe but plausible scenarios, and mapping and testing those services is what equips the firm to establish whether it can stay within tolerance and what changes may be needed to do so. [#TGT:0f14e9411e03a950] Linking these points, the same impact tolerance benchmarks that guide incident-time choices should also be used by boards and senior management to prioritise investment and to put recovery and response arrangements in place ahead of time, so that the firm’s mapped and tested capability aligns with staying within tolerance under stress. [#SRC:51a4e8e33523d5d5][#TGT:0f14e9411e03a950]","Impact tolerances provide a standard which boards and senior management should use for prioritising investment and making recovery and response arrangements (see Chapters 4 to 6 of this SS). They may be helpful in informing decision-making during operational disruptions, when they would be considered alongside other information relevant to managing an incident effectively.",The Operational Resilience Parts 17 require firms to ensure they are able to deliver their important business services within impact tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios. Mapping and testing the delivery of important business services will equip firms to establish whether and how they can remain within impact tolerances.,DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,51a4e8e33523d5d5,0f14e9411e03a950,,,51a4e8e33523d5d5,0f14e9411e03a950,,,,,HV0129,6c71c40cbac54bce,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

f785a281ba3c0bbc,"When a firm’s recovery plan includes a communication plan for informing internal and external stakeholders during the recovery process, what governance alignment is expected for that communication plan, and what specific communication objectives should the plan address (including handling negative market reaction and wider financial system impact)?","A firm’s recovery plan is expected to embed a communication plan that both sets out what the firm will communicate during recovery and is governed in a way that aligns with how recovery actions are authorised and controlled. [#TGT:bb8b61ee7ed6c85d] Specifically, the governance procedures for the communication plan should be documented within the recovery plan and should match the governance procedures used to invoke the recovery plan itself, while also being consistent with the firm’s broader corporate governance for communications. [#SRC:b3cab0b6630c112c] If the communication plan’s governance differs from either the recovery-plan invocation governance or the firm’s wider communications governance, the firm should explain those differences. [#SRC:b3cab0b6630c112c] In terms of content and objectives, the communication plan should provide a clear strategy for disseminating timely and appropriate information to stakeholders, including both internal and external audiences, throughout the firm’s recovery process. [#TGT:bb8b61ee7ed6c85d] The plan should also address how the firm will manage potential negative market reactions to recovery options, how it will mitigate potential impacts of recovery options on the firm’s financial position and franchise, and how the approach is designed to minimise broader impacts on the financial system. [#TGT:bb8b61ee7ed6c85d]","Governance procedures for the firm’s communication plan (see ‘ (ix) Communication plan ’ below) should be captured by the recovery plan and be consistent with the governance procedures for invoking the recovery plan itself. They should also be consistent with the firm’s wider corporate governance for communications. Where this is not the case, the differences should be explained.","The recovery plan should include a communication plan to ensure that there is a clear strategy for managing the dissemination of timely and appropriate information to stakeholders (both internal and external) during the firm’s recovery process. In particular, firms should consider how they will manage any negative market reaction to recovery options, mitigate the potential impact of recovery options on the firm’s financial position and franchise, and detail how the approach seeks to minimise the impact on the financial system more widely.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,b3cab0b6630c112c,bb8b61ee7ed6c85d,,,b3cab0b6630c112c,bb8b61ee7ed6c85d,,,,,HV0130,f785a281ba3c0bbc,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

d9c3713da950deb5,"When a firm is ensuring that the calculation of the probability distribution forecast produced by its internal model meets the specified compliance standard, what additional expectation applies regarding the principles for the methods and assumptions used in the internal model, and what must be done to demonstrate compliance?","A firm must ensure that its internal model—specifically including how it calculates the probability distribution forecast it generates—complies with the specified set of requirements. [#TGT:3ed819cc35a6fc9d] In doing so, the firm must also ensure that the methods and assumptions used in the internal model adhere to the principles set out in the Statistical Quality Standards (SQS) for internal models. [#SRC:f9ebadff53a4bf82] Beyond meeting those substantive requirements, the firm has an explicit evidencing obligation: compliance with the SQS requirements must be demonstrated to the PRA. [#SRC:f9ebadff53a4bf82] Practically, this means the firm’s compliance approach should link the probability distribution forecast calculation back to the underlying methods and assumptions and show that those methods and assumptions follow the relevant SQS principles, and then provide evidence of that compliance to the PRA. [#SRC:f9ebadff53a4bf82] The combined expectation is therefore twofold: (1) ensure the internal model’s probability distribution forecast calculation complies with the stated requirements, and (2) evidence to the PRA that the internal model’s methods and assumptions comply with the SQS principles. [#TGT:3ed819cc35a6fc9d] [#SRC:f9ebadff53a4bf82]",The Statistical Quality Standards (SQS) for internal models in Solvency Capital Requirement – Internal Models 11 and Solvency Capital Requirement – Internal Models 16.2 set out requirements on the principles that the methods and assumptions used in the internal model must adhere to.
