Compliance with those requirements must be evidenced to the PRA.,"A firm must ensure that its internal model and, in particular, the calculation of the probability distribution forecast generated by it, complies with 11.2 to 11.13 .",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,f9ebadff53a4bf82,3ed819cc35a6fc9d,,,f9ebadff53a4bf82,3ed819cc35a6fc9d,,,,,HV0131,d9c3713da950deb5,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

6c636537df6c2f62,"When a firm with a matching adjustment permission is determining technical provisions in a currency where the PRA does not publish the relevant calibration inputs, how must the firm ensure its proposed fundamental spread approach captures differences in credit quality by rating notch for an assigned asset that maps to credit quality steps 1 to 5?","In that situation, the firm must both (i) develop and defend its own technical information for the fundamental spread and (ii) apply a rating-notch adjustment for relevant assigned assets. Where the PRA does not publish the technical information needed for the MA calculation in a particular currency, it becomes the firm’s responsibility to propose technical information that meets Solvency II requirements and to justify the approach to its supervisor. [#SRC:8453fefed49631c2] In addition, for any assigned asset that has a credit rating or internal credit assessment of a comparable standard mapping to credit quality steps 1 to 5 (inclusive), the firm must adjust the fundamental spread that would otherwise be derived from the asset’s credit quality step so that it reflects the corresponding rating notch. [#TGT:9fdf13a401180fa3] The practical implication is that the firm’s self-proposed technical information cannot stop at a credit-quality-step level if it is to be used for such assigned assets; it must be capable (where possible and appropriate) of being adjusted to capture differences in credit quality by rating notch. [#SRC:8453fefed49631c2] The firm should be prepared to explain to its supervisor how its proposed calibration and the required notch-level adjustment work together to produce an MA fundamental spread that meets the applicable requirements. [#SRC:8453fefed49631c2][#TGT:9fdf13a401180fa3]","For the purposes of determining TPs, the FS calibrations used in the MA calculation are, in most cases, provided by the PRA in technical information produced in accordance with Matching Adjustment 4.10 to 4.15 . Where a firm has TPs in a particular currency for which the PRA does not publish technical information, it is the firm’s responsibility to propose technical information that complies with Solvency II requirements, and to justify this approach to its supervisor. 5 Firms are required to adjust this technical information (where possible and appropriate) to allow the FS to capture differences in credit quality by rating notch ( Matching Adjustment 6 ). Firms are required to apply additions to the FS for assets with highly predictable (HP) cash flows (as per Matching Adjustment 4.16 ) and can apply any further additions to the FS that they consider necessary to ensure it covers all risks retained by the firm (as per Matching Adjustment 4.17 ). No similar technical information is provided in order to calculate the SCR and the PRA expects firms to consider if and how any adjustments to the technical information, and additions to the FS, used to calculate TPs need to be updated in stress conditions.","Where an assigned asset has a credit rating or internal credit assessment of a comparable standard (within the meaning of 7.1(1) ) mapping to credit quality steps 1 to 5 (inclusive), a firm with a matching adjustment permission must make an adjustment to the fundamental spread derived from the credit quality step attributed to that asset in order to reflect the corresponding rating notch , in accordance with 6.3 and 6.4 .",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,8453fefed49631c2,9fdf13a401180fa3,,,8453fefed49631c2,9fdf13a401180fa3,,,,,HV0132,6c636537df6c2f62,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

34e2b915257abecc,"When assessing whether a special purpose vehicle located in Gibraltar or a third country can be treated as meeting the relevant regulatory expectations, what conditions must be satisfied regarding (i) oversight by a supervisory authority and equivalence of requirements, and (ii) the governance arrangements expected of a UK ISPV in light of the risks assumed and the authorised regulated activity?","To treat a special purpose vehicle in Gibraltar or a third country as meeting the relevant expectations, you must confirm both its external regulatory status and the governance standard that would apply in the UK context. [#SRC:012c29b081ac0f05] Specifically, the Gibraltar/third-country vehicle must be regulated by a supervisory authority in Gibraltar or that third country, and it must comply with requirements that are equivalent to the specified set of Insurance Special Purpose Vehicles requirements. [#SRC:012c29b081ac0f05] In parallel, the benchmark governance expectation for a UK ISPV is that it has an effective system of governance designed to ensure sound and prudent management, and that this system is appropriate to the nature, scale, and complexity of the risks the UK ISPV assumes as well as the regulated activity for which it is authorised. [#TGT:d90fd8705cd51108] Read together, this means an equivalence assessment for a non-UK vehicle should not stop at confirming supervision and formal equivalence; it should also consider whether the vehicle’s governance arrangements would meet the UK ISPV standard of effectiveness and proportionality to its risk profile and authorised activity. [#SRC:012c29b081ac0f05] [#TGT:d90fd8705cd51108]","(2) in the case of a special purpose vehicle in Gibraltar or a third country , it is regulated by a supervisory authority in Gibraltar or a third country , and complies with requirements equivalent to those set out in Insurance Special Purpose Vehicles 2 , 2A to 2D , and 5A.1 to 5A.4 .","A UK ISPV must have an effective system of governance which provides for the sound and prudent management of the UK ISPV and which is appropriate to the nature, scale and complexity of the risks it assumes and the regulated activity for which it is authorised.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,012c29b081ac0f05,d90fd8705cd51108,,,012c29b081ac0f05,d90fd8705cd51108,,,,,HV0133,34e2b915257abecc,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

3bdf1c57377df0f9,"For an RFTS application, who runs the overall process, and who sends the financial resources certificate to the court if the transferee is only regulated by the FCA, considering the regulators’ agreement on how they coordinate shared-interest functions?","The PRA runs the overall RFTS process, but the FCA takes over issuing the financial resources certificate to the court when the transferee is an FCA solo regulated entity, within a wider coordination arrangement between the two regulators for RFTS-related functions. [#TGT:39a1985ef6854457] In general, the PRA leads the process for the RFTS and is responsible for specific regulatory functions connected with RFTS applications, including providing certificates. [#TGT:39a1985ef6854457] The stated exception is that, if the transferee is an FCA solo regulated entity, the FCA issues the certificate of financial resources to the court. [#TGT:39a1985ef6854457] This split of tasks aligns with the fact that both the PRA and the FCA have statutory functions in relation to RFTS and they maintain a Memorandum of Understanding that sets out each regulator’s role for functions involving common regulatory interest and explains how they intend to coordinate the exercise of those functions. [#SRC:5f2897ab41776611]","FSMA 5 also prescribes certain statutory functions in relation to RFTS for both the PRA and FCA. In accordance with FSMA, the PRA and the FCA maintain a Memorandum of Understanding 6 which describes each regulator’s role in relation to the exercise of its functions under FSMA relating to matters of common regulatory interest and how each regulator intends to ensure the co-ordinated exercise of such functions.","The PRA will lead the process for the RFTS. As described above, the PRA will also be responsible for specific regulatory functions connected with RFTS applications including the provision of certificates under section 111 of FSMA. The only exception to this is when the transferee is an FCA solo regulated entity. In this instance, the FCA will issue the certificate of financial resources to the court.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,5f2897ab41776611,39a1985ef6854457,,,5f2897ab41776611,39a1985ef6854457,,,,,HV0134,3bdf1c57377df0f9,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

34051549c629fc2a,"If a firm chooses to produce one integrated document that combines its liquidity contingency plan (contingency funding plan) and its recovery plan, how should it align scenario testing in that recovery plan with existing stress testing capabilities, and what standard must the recovery-plan scenarios meet?","When a firm integrates its liquidity contingency plan (contingency funding plan) with its recovery plan into a single document, it should design scenario testing for the recovery plan in a way that leverages its established stress testing capabilities while still ensuring the recovery-plan scenarios are fit for purpose. [#TGT:d6da2dce246d82de] In practice, firms are encouraged to make their scenario-testing approach consistent with existing stress testing used for the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) and the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP), and where relevant may also draw on work performed for the Bank’s previous concurrent stress test exercises. [#SRC:62cb42c43841e1d5] Even when leveraging those existing capabilities within an integrated document intended to support coherent alerting and response to liquidity stress, the firm should not treat reuse as sufficient by itself; it must ensure that the scenarios included in the recovery plan are relevant and sufficiently severe for testing the recovery plan. [#SRC:62cb42c43841e1d5] This approach supports the objective of a coherent process and risk management framework that the integrated-document expectation is intended to promote. [#TGT:d6da2dce246d82de]","Firms are encouraged to ensure their approach to scenario testing is consistent with – and leverage – their existing stress testing capabilities, such as those used for the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) and the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP). Where relevant, this can include work done for the Bank’s previous concurrent stress test exercises (further detail on the interaction between these regimes is included in ‘ (xiii) Interaction with other relevant regimes and requirements ’ below). However, firms should ensure scenarios included in their recovery plan are relevant and sufficiently severe for testing the recovery plan.","Firms are strongly encouraged to combine their liquidity contingency plan 16 (also known as a contingency funding plan) and their recovery plan into one integrated document. This would ensure that the firm has a coherent process for being alerted to and addressing a liquidity stress and helps to ensure a coherent risk management framework. The PRA recognises that there may be some instances when it is necessary to maintain separate documents (eg due to requirements of local regulators), but expects this to be the exception and that any separate documents should be consistent with each other.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,62cb42c43841e1d5,d6da2dce246d82de,,,62cb42c43841e1d5,d6da2dce246d82de,,,,,HV0135,34051549c629fc2a,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

178294b9c547ae34,"For a UK subsidiary of a group based outside of the UK, how should the recovery plan allocate governance and accountability so that (i) indicator monitoring and action are managed within a UK governance framework with clear escalation to group level, and (ii) a named executive under the SMR is accountable for the recovery plan and acts as the firm’s contact point with the authorities?","A UK subsidiary of a group based outside of the UK should structure its recovery plan so that UK-level governance for monitoring indicators and taking action is clearly defined, while also specifying when decisions are escalated to group level, and it should assign a single named executive under the SMR who is accountable for the recovery plan and related governance processes. [#SRC:540b8d2e62cc1fe2] The plan should include a UK governance framework that covers how indicators are monitored and how actions are triggered and managed, and for UK subsidiaries in non-UK groups it should also describe the points at which decisions would be escalated to group level. [#SRC:540b8d2e62cc1fe2] In parallel, because recovery planning is treated as a prescribed responsibility under the SMR, the firm should identify a named executive who is accountable for the recovery plan and resolution pack and who oversees the internal governance processes supporting them. [#TGT:084062e615cc02e8] That accountable executive director should also be identified as the firm’s contact point with the authorities on its recovery plan, and the PRA expects to hold this person accountable for the plan’s quality, usability for senior executives and board members in stress, improvements (including responding to PRA feedback), and engagement with the PRA on recovery planning matters. [#TGT:084062e615cc02e8] The subsidiary should also ensure it meets the SMR-related expectations on responsibilities referenced for such UK subsidiaries. [#SRC:540b8d2e62cc1fe2]","(vi) The plan should include a UK governance framework for monitoring the indicators and taking action where appropriate. For UK subsidiaries of groups based outside of the UK, in meeting expectations set out in Chapter 2 (viii) , the PRA expects firms to set out when decisions would be escalated to group level. In addition, the PRA expects UK subsidiaries of groups based outside of the UK to meet requirements set out in Chapter 2 (xiii) (c) in relation to responsibilities under the SMR.","Firms are reminded that recovery planning is a prescribed responsibility under the SMR which means that there should be a named executive at each firm that is accountable for the recovery plan and resolution pack and for overseeing the internal processes regarding their governance. 18 Firms should identify the accountable executive director responsible for the firm’s recovery plan and for acting as the firm’s contact point with the authorities on its recovery plan. The PRA has observed that this is typically the CEO, CFO or CRO. The PRA will hold this person accountable for the quality of the recovery plan, for the plan being structured so as to be usable by senior executives and board members in a stress, for making improvements to the recovery plan (including in response to the PRA’s feedback) and for the firm’s engagement with the PRA on recovery planning issues.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,540b8d2e62cc1fe2,084062e615cc02e8,,,540b8d2e62cc1fe2,084062e615cc02e8,,,,,HV0136,178294b9c547ae34,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

db62c029d8c337c9,"If a firm is in a group, what does it need to have in place at group level to check whether important group business services can stay within impact tolerance during a major disruption, and when can it ignore the related group-level requirements because the parent company is based in a designated overseas jurisdiction for insurance group supervision?","When a firm is a member of a group in scope, it must make sure that the group has strategies, processes and systems that let the firm assess whether important group business services could stay within the impact tolerance if there is a severe but plausible disruption to operations. [#TGT:43a647fe4cce5cd9] Separately, there is a situation where certain group-level provisions do not apply: this is when the firm is a member of a group covered by the specified group category, the group’s parent undertaking has its head office in a third country that is an overseas jurisdiction designated for insurance group supervision (as described), and the stated condition about the application of the relevant paragraph is met. [#SRC:b6b6500b2b9939c8] So the firm should (1) confirm it is in the relevant type of group and (2) check the parent undertaking’s head-office location and whether it is in a designated overseas jurisdiction with the stated paragraph applying; only then can it treat those group-level provisions as not applying. [#SRC:b6b6500b2b9939c8] If that carve-out does not apply, the firm still needs the group-level capability to perform the impact-tolerance assessment for important group business services under severe but plausible disruption conditions. [#TGT:43a647fe4cce5cd9]","Where a firm is a member of a group covered by 2.1(3) , 22.2 , 22.3 and 22.4 do not apply if, the third country in which the group's parent undertaking has its head office is an overseas jurisdiction designated under regulation 11 in relation to regulation 14 of the IRPR regulations in respect of insurance group supervision and paragraph (3) of regulation 14 of the IRPR regulations applies.","Where a firm is a member of a group covered by 2.1(1) , 2.1(2) or, subject to 22.5 , 2.1(3) the firm must ensure that the strategies, processes and systems at the level of the group of which it is a member enable the firm to assess whether important group business services at the level of the group could remain within the impact tolerance in the event of a severe but plausible disruption to its operations.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,b6b6500b2b9939c8,43a647fe4cce5cd9,,,b6b6500b2b9939c8,43a647fe4cce5cd9,,,,,HV0137,db62c029d8c337c9,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

e4e335cafbf931c3,"When a firm is determining its basic own funds and needs to reduce them because it holds participations in a financial and credit institution above the stated percentage threshold, what reduction is required and what should the firm do if it cannot apply the straightforward approach for allocating the resulting deduction across tiers of own funds?","In determining its basic own funds, a firm is required to make a reduction when it has participations in a financial and credit institution that exceed the specified threshold relative to the referenced items. [#TGT:0627964a494e4b18] Specifically, the firm must reduce its basic own funds by the full value of the participations that exceed 10% of the items included in the listed components. [#TGT:0627964a494e4b18] Because this reduction can create a deduction from own-funds that then needs to be reflected appropriately within the firm’s own-funds structure, the firm should also use the supporting guidelines for performing the calculations required by the relevant own-funds calculation framework. [#SRC:f70061d7218c187e] If a deduction from own-funds is necessary and the firm cannot apply the straightforward approach for allocating that deduction, it should follow the specified guideline that is intended to identify which tier of own-funds the adjustment should apply to. [#SRC:f70061d7218c187e] This links the mandatory reduction in basic own funds for qualifying participations above the threshold with the procedural expectation for handling cases where tier-allocation of the resulting deduction is not straightforward. [#SRC:f70061d7218c187e]","Firms should observe Guidelines 4 and 5 which support the carrying out of the calculations required by Own Funds 3K . Where a deduction from own-funds is necessary, and where a straightforward application of Own Funds 3K.5 is not possible, firms should follow Guideline 6 to identify the tier of own-funds to which the adjustment should apply.","A firm must, for the purpose of determining its basic own funds , reduce its basic own funds by the full value of participations , as referred to in 3K.6 , in a financial and credit institution that exceeds 10% of items included in 3A.1(1)(a) , 3A.1(1)(b) , 3A.1(1)(d) and 3A.1(1)(f) .",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,f70061d7218c187e,0627964a494e4b18,,,f70061d7218c187e,0627964a494e4b18,,,,,HV0138,e4e335cafbf931c3,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

23b812089577d748,"When setting up governance and prudential risk management arrangements, what must an insurer’s risk appetite/tolerance framework cover, and how must the firm’s risk-management system address risks across both individual and aggregated exposures on an ongoing basis?","An insurer should treat its risk appetite or tolerance as a core element of an effective governance and prudential risk management framework, and it must be supported by a risk-management system that continuously identifies, measures, monitors, manages, and reports risks both per-risk and in aggregate, including how risks relate to each other. [#SRC:e007010cf752bc53] [#TGT:9f2e6ec1c2bc29ca] To be complete, the insurer needs (i) a defined risk appetite/tolerance and (ii) a process and systems that operationalize that appetite through end-to-end risk handling and escalation to management or the board. [#SRC:e007010cf752bc53] The risk-management system must comprise strategies, processes, and reporting procedures that enable continuous risk identification, measurement, monitoring, management, and reporting, covering risks the firm is exposed to or could be exposed to. [#TGT:9f2e6ec1c2bc29ca] It must also address risks at an individual level and at an aggregated level, and capture interdependencies among those risks, so that aggregation and linkage effects are visible rather than assessed in isolation. [#TGT:9f2e6ec1c2bc29ca] In parallel, the insurer must have appropriate systems to convey risk information to management or the board, aligning reporting and escalation with the risk appetite/tolerance and the broader governance system. [#SRC:e007010cf752bc53]","Conditions Governing Business Chapters 2 and 3 , supplemented by Non-Solvency II Firms – Governance Chapters 2 , 3 and 7 require an insurer to establish an effective system of governance and prudential risk management systems. An insurer is required to have a risk appetite or tolerance for risk, a process to identify, measure, and monitor risk and appropriate systems to convey information to management or the board.","(1) A firm must establish, implement, and maintain an effective risk-management system comprising strategies, processes and reporting procedures necessary to identify, measure, monitor, manage and report on a continuous basis the risks, at an individual and at an aggregated level, to which it is or could be exposed, and their interdependencies.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,e007010cf752bc53,9f2e6ec1c2bc29ca,,,e007010cf752bc53,9f2e6ec1c2bc29ca,,,,,HV0139,23b812089577d748,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

3f12528d544848aa,"For a contract where further specified premiums are payable by the policyholder, the contract is not a linked long-term contract of insurance, the policyholder is eligible to participate in any established surplus, and benefits (other than those arising from a distribution of surplus) are fixed from the outset by reference to the total premiums payable, when may an alternative valuation method be used and what outcome must be demonstrated for reserves?","In the scenario described—where further specified premiums are payable by the policyholder under a contract that is not a linked long-term contract of insurance, the policyholder can participate in any established surplus, and the relevant benefits are set from the outset by reference to the total premiums payable—the valuation approach applied to determine reserves may depart from the otherwise described method only if a specific safeguard is met. [#TGT:b59bd9a0020ac30e] Specifically, an alternative valuation method is permitted only where it can be demonstrated that using the alternative produces reserves that are not lower in aggregate than the reserves that would result from applying the method that would otherwise be used. [#SRC:0e0944866773b598] This means the firm must be able to evidence, on an aggregate basis, that the alternative method does not reduce the overall level of reserves compared with the baseline method, even though the contract features include ongoing specified premiums and surplus participation with benefits determined by reference to total premiums. [#TGT:b59bd9a0020ac30e] The key compliance condition is therefore not the contract design itself, but the requirement to demonstrate equivalence or conservatism in aggregate reserves relative to the baseline method before relying on the alternative approach. [#SRC:0e0944866773b598]","An alternative valuation method to that described in 9.1 to 9.3 may be used where it can be demonstrated that the alternative method results in reserves no less, in aggregate, than would result from use of the method described in 9.1 to 9.3 .","Where further specified premiums are payable by the policyholder under a contract (not being a linked long-term contract of insurance ) under which the policyholder is eligible to participate in any established surplus and benefits (other than benefits arising from a distribution of surplus) are determined from the outset in relation to the total premiums payable thereunder, then, subject to 9.4 and 10 :",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,0e0944866773b598,b59bd9a0020ac30e,,,0e0944866773b598,b59bd9a0020ac30e,,,,,HV0140,3f12528d544848aa,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

89852cc551e51d85,"If a friendly society is transferring to another friendly society and an actuary’s report from the transferee is needed (or might be demanded) to show solvency or an excess of assets over liabilities, when could the PRA ask for an extra report after members have voted, and what extra steps might that cause?","In a transfer to another friendly society, the PRA’s starting point is that an actuary’s report from the transferee is required in one set of circumstances to confirm it will meet the necessary margin of solvency, and the PRA may require an actuary’s report in another set of circumstances to confirm it will have an excess of assets over liabilities. [#TGT:ba58567331c57f62] Where such reports are required, the PRA may also ask for a supplementary report in certain instances, such as when there have been material financial or other developments after the members’ vote but before the confirmation hearing. [#SRC:fc9e80a67deee879] The PRA will look at the procedural impact of requesting that supplementary report on a case-by-case basis. [#SRC:fc9e80a67deee879] If the supplementary report reaches different conclusions from the first reports, the PRA notes this may mean more communications with affected members who can vote and/or more advertising. [#SRC:fc9e80a67deee879] If the changed conclusions are material enough, it may also result in needing another member vote. [#SRC:fc9e80a67deee879]","Where the reports detailed in paragraphs 4.5 and 4.6 are required, the PRA may request in certain instances that supplementary reports are produced, for example where there have been material financial or other developments subsequent to the members’ vote and prior to the confirmation hearing. In such instances, the PRA will consider the specific procedural implications of requesting a supplementary report on a case-by-case basis. For example, where the conclusions in the supplementary reports differ from those in the first reports the PRA notes this may necessitate further communications with affected members eligible to vote and/or additional advertising. Depending on the materiality of the conclusions reached, it may also lead to the requirement for a further member vote.","For a transfer to another friendly society, if the conditions of 87(1) and 87(2) of the Friendly Societies Act 1992 are met, a report is required from the appropriate actuary of the transferee to confirm that it will meet the necessary margin of solvency. Where the conditions of 87(1) and 87(3) are met, the PRA may require a report from the appropriate actuary of the transferee to confirm that it will have an excess of assets over liabilities.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,fc9e80a67deee879,ba58567331c57f62,,,fc9e80a67deee879,ba58567331c57f62,,,,,HV0141,89852cc551e51d85,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

4444ef76b67c9f81,"When a firm seeks a subsequent variation of its MA permission, what must the written application include regarding documentary evidence and how must changes be presented and confirmed, including any specific method for signposting changes?","For a subsequent variation of MA permission, the firm is expected to submit a written application that includes both a short description of the proposed changes and documentary evidence that has been updated from the suite supporting the existing permission. [#TGT:84f7883e3f0125f9] In addition, the PRA will still require the application to be accompanied by documentary evidence, and where the application is a change in scope, the changes must be signposted in the manner described for that purpose. [#SRC:974d2778f8f27567] Practically, the updated documentary evidence should be prepared so that any differences from what was previously submitted are clearly highlighted using a ‘track changes’ approach. [#TGT:84f7883e3f0125f9] The firm should also include, within its short description of the changes, an explicit confirmation that all changes to its application have been displayed as ‘track changes’ and that no other changes have been made beyond those shown. [#TGT:84f7883e3f0125f9] This combination of a written application with accompanying evidence, plus clearly signposted amendments (including for change in scope applications), is intended to reduce administrative and operational burden while ensuring the PRA can readily identify what has changed. [#SRC:974d2778f8f27567] [#TGT:84f7883e3f0125f9]","The PRA will still require firms to submit a written application as set out in Chapter 2 of this SoP, including accompanying documentary evidence and, for a change in scope application, changes signposted as described in paragraph 2.18 of this SoP.","To ease the administrative and operational burden on both firms and the PRA, the PRA expects a firm to update the suite of documentary evidence covering its initial MA permission, for each subsequent variation of that permission. Applications for a variation of MA permission should cover a short description of the proposed changes together with an updated suite of documentary evidence, where the changes to this evidence from that previously submitted to the PRA to support the existing permission are clearly signposted using ‘track changes’. The firm should clearly confirm, in its short description of the changes, that all changes to its application have been displayed as ‘track changes’ and that no other changes have been made.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,974d2778f8f27567,84f7883e3f0125f9,,,974d2778f8f27567,84f7883e3f0125f9,,,,,HV0142,4444ef76b67c9f81,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

ee770fb3dba5d8d8,"If a firm learns that another company in its group (not covered by Own Funds 5) plans to issue something the firm wants to count as basic own funds for the group SCR, what does the firm need to tell the PRA, and what happens if the firm changes the details before the item is issued?","The firm must write to the PRA as soon as it becomes aware that another member of its group (which is not subject to Own Funds 5) intends to issue an item that the firm intends to include within the basic own funds forming the own funds eligible for the group SCR. [#TGT:a69fc1cead7ea616] If the firm has already made that initial notification and then, before the item is issued, it proposes to change any of the information it previously submitted, it must send another written notification covering the change, and it must do this without delay. [#SRC:b15834f057327c97] Put together, the timing is important: the first message is triggered by the firm becoming aware of the issuing undertaking’s intention, and the second message is triggered by the firm proposing changes to what it already told the PRA during the period after the initial notice but prior to issuance. [#TGT:a69fc1cead7ea616] [#SRC:b15834f057327c97]","If after an initial notification under 6.2 , but prior to an item’s issuance, a firm proposes to change the information previously submitted, it must provide a further written notification of that change without delay.","(1) Subject to 6.5 , a firm must notify the PRA in writing of the intention of another member of its group which is not subject to Own Funds 5 to issue an item which it intends to include within the basic own funds forming the own funds eligible for the group SCR , as soon as it becomes aware of the intention of the issuing undertaking .",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,b15834f057327c97,a69fc1cead7ea616,,,b15834f057327c97,a69fc1cead7ea616,,,,,HV0143,ee770fb3dba5d8d8,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

a776cc115877ed4c,"If an asset has both economic risk and event risk, what approach should a firm follow, and if it has good data to model event-driven cash flow swings more carefully, what level of provision does the PRA say is broadly in line with an 85th-percentile outcome for a fatter-tailed distribution?","Where an asset exposure includes both economic and event risk, the firm should use the standard approach that matches the dominant risk in that exposure. [#SRC:957d2122eefbf855] Separately, if the firm has more complete credible data that supports more sophisticated modelling of event-driven cash flow variability, the PRA indicates that these event-driven risks are more likely to be represented by fatter-tailed distributions and explains a practical equivalence for setting an adequate provision. [#TGT:24cba8bb8769696c] The PRA considers that a provision equal to one quarter of the difference in MA benefit between median cash flows and worst cash flows is broadly equivalent to targeting the 85th percentile of a fatter-tailed distribution. [#TGT:24cba8bb8769696c] The PRA further indicates that this level of provision would likely demonstrate adequate provision for the additional retained cash flow variability risks. [#TGT:24cba8bb8769696c] Putting these together, the firm should first decide which standard approach applies by identifying the dominant risk (economic or event) for the asset, and then—if it is using credible data to support more sophisticated modelling of event-driven variability—use the quarter-of-the-median-to-worst MA benefit difference as the PRA’s benchmark for adequacy against a fatter-tailed 85th-percentile target. [#SRC:957d2122eefbf855] [#TGT:24cba8bb8769696c]","The PRA has set out expectations in paragraphs 5.23 to 5.25 below for standard approaches for economic and event risk exposures. For assets with both economic and event risk exposures, firms should follow the approach for the dominant risks. For pooled asset exposures where the underlying assets are exposed to economic risks but where there is sufficient evidence of predictability, firms may propose to apply the standard approach to the FS addition for event risks.","The PRA considers that event-driven cash flow variability risks are more likely to be best represented by fatter-tailed distributions. Where more complete credible data becomes available to support more sophisticated modelling, the PRA considers that a provision of one quarter of the difference in MA benefit from median to worst cash flows is broadly equivalent to targeting the 85th percentile of a fatter-tailed distribution and that this would likely demonstrate adequate provision for the additional retained cash flow variability risks.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,957d2122eefbf855,24cba8bb8769696c,,,957d2122eefbf855,24cba8bb8769696c,,,,,HV0144,a776cc115877ed4c,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

04550da1629d09ad,"If a firm is small and has a simple business model, can its solvent exit analysis be shorter, and what parts of the analysis are likely to be smaller or simpler compared with a bigger, more complex firm?","Yes. The amount of detail in a solvent exit analysis is expected to match the firm’s nature, scale, and complexity, so a smaller and simpler firm can reasonably prepare a shorter analysis than a larger, more complex firm. [#SRC:2a3666ddbe534cd1][#TGT:81ad87350f8e63bb] For a smaller firm with a simple business model, the analysis may be shorter because it may need to cover a smaller range of solvent exit indicators, set out a more limited number of solvent exit actions, and describe simpler governance arrangements. [#TGT:81ad87350f8e63bb] This is an application of the proportionality expectation: the analysis should not be more detailed than is justified by the firm’s scale and complexity, but it should still reflect the firm’s own indicators, actions, and governance in a way that fits its circumstances. [#SRC:2a3666ddbe534cd1][#TGT:81ad87350f8e63bb] Where a firm is larger or more complex, the same proportionality principle implies that more detail may be needed to address a broader set of indicators, actions, and governance arrangements. [#SRC:2a3666ddbe534cd1][#TGT:81ad87350f8e63bb]","The level of detail in the solvent exit analysis should be proportionate to the nature, scale, and complexity of the firm. 18 A firm may find it helpful to include the solvent exit analysis as a discrete section in its recovery plan, but may set out the solvent exit analysis separately if the firm finds it appropriate","18. For example, a smaller firm with a simple business model may produce a shorter solvent exit analysis than a larger, more complex firm, given that the smaller firm may have a smaller range of solvent exit indicators, a more limited number of solvent exit actions, and simpler governance arrangements.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,2a3666ddbe534cd1,81ad87350f8e63bb,,,2a3666ddbe534cd1,81ad87350f8e63bb,,,,,HV0145,04550da1629d09ad,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

742e4ef5df6fdb52,"If the Chief Actuary is choosing a method for the TMTP projected risk margin portion and dynamic portion, what does the method need to match, and how should it reflect how complex the firm’s insurance and reinsurance risks are?","For the TMTP method used to calculate the projected risk margin portion and the dynamic portion, the Chief Actuary may choose an appropriate methodology, but it must be consistent with the calculation of Technical Provisions and with the relevant principles referenced for Technical Provisions further requirements. [#SRC:150a80115b4cbf41] Separately, the firm must calculate technical provisions using methods that are proportionate to the nature, scale, and complexity of the risks underlying its insurance and reinsurance obligations. [#TGT:df6dca1e4bdffda8] Putting these together, the Chief Actuary’s TMTP methodology choice should fit within the firm’s Technical Provisions calculation framework and principles, while also being applied in a way that is proportionate to the firm’s underlying risk profile (how big and complex the risks are, and what kind they are). [#SRC:150a80115b4cbf41] [#TGT:df6dca1e4bdffda8]","For the TMTP method when calculating the projected risk margin portion and dynamic portion as set out in Transitional Measures on Technical Provisions 5.2 , the Chief Actuary may select appropriate methodologies consistent with the calculation of Technical Provisions and the principles set out in chapter 27 of the Technical Provisions – Further Requirements Part of the PRA Rulebook.","A firm must use methods to calculate technical provisions which are proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of the risks underlying their insurance and reinsurance obligations.",DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,150a80115b4cbf41,df6dca1e4bdffda8,,,150a80115b4cbf41,df6dca1e4bdffda8,,,,,HV0146,742e4ef5df6fdb52,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

05d2357faeb548e9,"For a G-SII making disclosures that fall within Titles II and III, what is the required publication approach and what is the latest deadline after the end of the relevant period for making the specific disclosures that are required under the referenced disclosure obligation?","A G-SII must both (i) follow the prescribed publication approach for disclosures that fall within Titles II and III and (ii) meet a specific end-of-period deadline for the particular set of disclosures in scope. Institutions are required to publish the disclosures required under Titles II and III using the manner specified in the referenced publication framework. [#TGT:a2135b9576433803] Separately, for G-SIIs, the information that is required under the referenced disclosure obligation must be disclosed no later than four months after the end of the period to which that information relates. [#SRC:7d9ddc368d96439f] Read together, where the G-SII’s relevant disclosures are within Titles II and III and include the specified information, the institution should publish those disclosures using the stated manner while ensuring that the specified information is made public within the four-month window measured from the end of the relevant reporting period. [#TGT:a2135b9576433803] [#SRC:7d9ddc368d96439f]","By way of derogation from the second paragraph of Article 433, G-SIIs shall disclose the information required under Article 441 within four months after the end of the period to which the information relates.","Institutions shall publish the disclosures required under Titles II and III in the manner set out in Articles 433a , 433b and 433c .",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,7d9ddc368d96439f,a2135b9576433803,,,7d9ddc368d96439f,a2135b9576433803,,,,,HV0147,05d2357faeb548e9,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

ea7de73af61bc865,"If a critical third party has to show regulators it can meet the requirements, what does it need to do with what it learns from operational incidents and from testing and exercising (including testing and exercising done under a specific framework) to support that showing?","To support showing regulators that it can meet the requirements, a critical third party should be able to point to implemented improvements that come from what it learned during operational incidents and during testing and exercising. [#TGT:2d682f43e1f6ff70] The relevant expectation is not just to run tests or note incident outcomes, but to implement the lessons learned from CTP operational incidents and from any testing and exercising it undertakes, expressly including testing and exercising carried out under the referenced framework. [#SRC:ea54bf2b51940c0a] In other words, the demonstration to regulators should connect the “learning” sources (incidents and exercises) to real actions taken (changes put in place), because the ability to demonstrate compliance is about evidencing capability, not merely describing intentions. [#TGT:2d682f43e1f6ff70] This approach should cover lessons from all testing and exercising the critical third party performs, and it should not exclude the testing and exercising undertaken under the specified framework, since those are explicitly within scope of the lessons-to-implementation requirement. [#SRC:ea54bf2b51940c0a]","(4) implementing lessons learned from CTP operational incidents and any testing and exercising undertaken, including but not limited to that undertaken in accordance with 5 ;",A critical third party must be able to demonstrate to the regulators its ability to comply with this Part.,DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,ea54bf2b51940c0a,2d682f43e1f6ff70,,,ea54bf2b51940c0a,2d682f43e1f6ff70,,,,,HV0148,ea7de73af61bc865,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

e94e94961406c1d2,"After the PRA has granted a permission, if a firm expects it soon will not continue to meet the ongoing conditions attached to that permission and promptly notifies the PRA, what discretion does the PRA have regarding revoking or modifying the permission upon receiving such notifications?","Where a permission has been granted and the relevant conditions are treated as continuing obligations that must be met on an ongoing basis, the firm is expected to notify the PRA promptly if it does not, or anticipates it soon will not, continue to meet any of those conditions for as long as the permission remains effective. [#TGT:0df24170860e6ba3] When the PRA receives the notifications described in the specified notification paragraphs, it has discretion to decide not to revoke or modify the permission it granted, even though the notification relates to a potential or actual failure to continue meeting those ongoing conditions. [#SRC:75e4f6a4b365751b] In practice, this means the firm’s prompt notification about an expected or actual lapse in continuing conditions is an expected step during the life of the permission, but receipt of that notification does not automatically require revocation or modification; the PRA may choose to leave the permission unchanged. [#TGT:0df24170860e6ba3] [#SRC:75e4f6a4b365751b]",The PRA may decide not to revoke or modify a permission that it has granted when it receives the notifications set out in paragraphs 3.3 to 3.5 above.,"Unless otherwise stated, the conditions set out in PRA rules and in this SoP should be thought of as continuing conditions which firms need to satisfy on an ongoing basis. After the PRA has granted a permission, it expects that the firm promptly notifies it if it does not, or expects that it soon will not, continue to meet any of those conditions for as long as the permission remains effective.",DPEL,,professional,UKFIN,hard_enriched,75e4f6a4b365751b,0df24170860e6ba3,,,75e4f6a4b365751b,0df24170860e6ba3,,,,,HV0149,e94e94961406c1d2,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

7394abdceba58c95,"If the PRA is worried about a firm’s culture (like weak governance, bad incentives, low risk awareness, or people not challenging senior management), what extra step can it take to help spot concerns, and what does the PRA treat as a “sound risk culture” in that context?","Where the PRA is looking for signs of cultural weakness, it can use a skilled person report as an extra step to further help it identify concerns. [#TGT:a25861a4ea87d83f] This is relevant because the PRA’s culture assessment already focuses on specific areas—governance, incentives, risk awareness, and whether there is an ability to challenge senior management—so an additional report can be used to add depth to those same themes. [#SRC:c3370c674393dee1] In judging what “good” looks like, the PRA has contributed to supervisory guidance that describes a sound risk culture as one that supports appropriate risk awareness, behaviours, and judgements about risk-taking, and that operates within a strong risk governance framework. [#SRC:c3370c674393dee1] Taken together, the skilled person report functions as a practical mechanism the PRA may use to develop or confirm its view on whether the firm’s culture matches those sound-risk-culture characteristics, while also helping it pinpoint concerns tied to the factors the PRA considers when identifying cultural failings. [#SRC:c3370c674393dee1] Further detail on the report’s use is indicated as provided elsewhere. [#TGT:a25861a4ea87d83f]","The PRA considers a variety of factors to identify failings in culture, including governance, incentives, risk awareness, and the ability to challenge senior management. The PRA also contributed to development of the Financial Stability Board’s Guidance on Supervisory Interaction with Financial Institutions on Risk Culture 7 , which identified a sound risk culture as one that supports appropriate risk awareness, behaviours and judgements about risk-taking within a strong risk governance framework.",A skilled person report may also be used to further help the PRA identify concerns. Further details are given in the next section.,DPEL,,basic,UKFIN,hard_enriched,c3370c674393dee1,a25861a4ea87d83f,,,c3370c674393dee1,a25861a4ea87d83f,,,,,HV0150,7394abdceba58c95,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

704e8007566eba2b,"For the obligation to disclose appropriately information that the FCA or PRA would reasonably expect notice of, which persons are within scope given that the requirement applies only to a person in the specified set of categories?","The duty to disclose appropriately any information that the FCA or PRA would reasonably expect to be notified of applies only where the individual is within the limited scope described in the source passage. In other words, you must first confirm that the relevant individual is “a person in (2)(a), (b), (e) or (f)” because the source makes clear that the provision applies only to that defined group [#SRC:d1f59ce90997f3d1]. If the individual falls within that scope, then the target obligation applies: the person must make an appropriate disclosure of any information that the FCA or PRA would reasonably expect notice of [#TGT:34a5a857f0439e3b]. If the individual does not fall within the specified categories, the source indicates the provision does not apply to them, and therefore the disclosure obligation described in the target should not be treated as applying via that scoped provision [#SRC:d1f59ce90997f3d1]. Practically, compliance should (i) identify whether the person is within the specified categories, and (ii) for those in scope, ensure processes exist to identify information the FCA or PRA would reasonably expect and to disclose it appropriately [#TGT:34a5a857f0439e3b].","(4) 3.4 only applies to a person in (2)(a), (b), (e) or (f).",Senior Manager Conduct Rule 4: You must disclose appropriately any information of which the FCA or PRA would reasonably expect notice.,SCHEMA,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,d1f59ce90997f3d1,34a5a857f0439e3b,,,d1f59ce90997f3d1,34a5a857f0439e3b,,,,,HV0151,704e8007566eba2b,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

b48c7c47f3497d55,"When a firm discovers that it has breached MA eligibility conditions only after the breach has occurred, how must the firm determine when the two‑month remediation window begins, and how does that timing interact with the requirement to start reducing the MA if non-compliance continues beyond two months? In that scenario, what procedural steps should the firm take to remedy the breach (including where assets or liabilities fall outside the scope of the existing MA permission) and what must it do before stopping any MA reduction?","If a breach of MA eligibility conditions is only identified or confirmed after it occurred, the firm should treat the two‑month period for remedying the breach as starting when the breach is detected or confirmed to have happened, with the PRA assessing the circumstances case by case [#SRC:512217c01b854b7e]. The remedial actions required within that window depend on the breach’s features; for example, if assets or liabilities have been included that are outside the scope of the existing MA permission, the firm may need to remove them from the portfolio while it makes a new MA application [#SRC:512217c01b854b7e]. If the firm remains non-compliant on an ongoing basis such that it is required to reduce the MA, it must begin reducing the MA immediately once two months have elapsed from the date of non-compliance, applying a 10% reduction factor (in bps) and then an additional 10% for each further month of continued non-compliance, calculated against the unadjusted MA using the current level of MA [#TGT:e9a9fe36f36ae205]. Any reduction ceases once compliance is restored, and the firm is expected to discuss with its usual supervisory contact whether the breach has been satisfactorily resolved before removing the reduction [#TGT:e9a9fe36f36ae205].","The PRA will consider the circumstances of a firm’s possible breach of MA eligibility conditions on a case-by-case basis. In cases where a breach is reasonably only determined after the date it has occurred (eg either identified by the firm or notified to the firm by the PRA), the two month period to remedy a breach of the MA eligibility conditions starts from the point at which the breach is detected or confirmed to have happened. The action(s) required to remedy the breach within that period (and hence, subject to the considerations in paragraph 8.1B above, avoid a reduction in the MA) will also depend on the circumstances of the breach; for example, in the event of assets or liabilities being included in the portfolio that are not covered by the scope of the existing MA permission, the remedy could be to remove the assets or liabilities from the portfolio pending making a new MA application.","Where a firm is required to reduce the MA for ongoing non-compliance with the MA eligibility conditions, in accordance with Matching Adjustment 13.5 , the firm is required to reduce the MA (expressed in bps) by a factor of 10%, commencing immediately two months from the date of non-compliance (subject to paragraph 8.3 below). The firm will be required to continue to reduce the MA by an additional 10% for each further month that it remains non-compliant, where the reduction factor of 10% is applied to the level of unadjusted MA. The PRA notes that the MA referenced in the rule is dynamic; for the purposes of calculating the reduced MA benefit, the PRA expects a firm to use the current level of MA. The PRA will consider the features of the breach of MA eligibility conditions and the firm’s risk management framework on a case-by-case basis. As a result, the PRA may ultimately determine that the MA should be reduced by a factor higher than 10% each month, or, conversely, may be willing to adopt a more flexible approach through the use of its supervisory powers. A reduction of the MA will cease to apply once the firm restores compliance with MA eligibility conditions. The PRA expects that the firm will discuss with its usual supervisory contact whether a particular breach has been satisfactorily resolved before removing a reduction to its MA.",SCHEMA,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,512217c01b854b7e,e9a9fe36f36ae205,,,512217c01b854b7e,e9a9fe36f36ae205,,,,,HV0152,b48c7c47f3497d55,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

9bdadc01ea707d39,"If a society is being taken over (its business is transferred to an existing company), how should it work out the Statutory Cash Bonus using the latest balance sheet and the member’s shares on the Qualifying Day, especially if the Transfer Statement is sent near the year end and the Annual Report and Accounts (or half-yearly results) affect what counts as the latest balance sheet? Also, when can the PRA require that no bonus is paid or that a smaller bonus is paid?","For a takeover where a society transfers its business to an existing company, the society should calculate the Statutory Cash Bonus by taking the ratio of the society’s reserves to its total liability to members in respect of shares, as shown in the latest balance sheet, and applying that ratio to the value of the shares held by the member on the Qualifying Day [#TGT:6e6626d8e0f6b007]. The society should align this calculation with the transaction timing: if a Transfer Statement is approved and sent to members just before, or shortly after, the end of the society’s financial year, it matters that the Annual Report and Accounts for that year will have been published by the vesting date, which is when qualifying membership must be established and the bonus is due to be paid; in that situation, the “latest balance sheet” is the one published in the most recent Annual Accounts [#TGT:6e6626d8e0f6b007]. The same kind of timing issue may also arise when the society publishes half-yearly results [#TGT:6e6626d8e0f6b007]. Even if the calculation would otherwise produce a payment, the PRA may direct, based on what is equitable between members, that no Statutory Cash Bonus is paid or that a lesser amount is paid when it confirms the transfer in a takeover [#SRC:fc03d66ef75da373].","The PRA may direct, however, where it confirms a transfer of a society’s business to an existing company (ie only in a takeover), that no Statutory Cash Bonus is paid or that a lesser amount is paid than that referred to in paragraph 4.50 , having regard to what is equitable between the members.","The bonus is to be calculated as that proportion which the society’s reserves bear to its total liability to its members in respect of shares, as shown in the latest balance sheet of the society, applied to the value of the shares held by the member on the Qualifying Day. If a Transfer Statement is approved and sent to the members just before, or shortly after, the end of the financial year of the society, it will be important to note that the Annual Report and Accounts for the year will have been published by the vesting date, when qualifying membership has to be established and the bonus is due to be paid. In those circumstances, ‘the latest balance sheet of the society’ will be that published in the most recent Annual Accounts. The same considerations may apply when a society publishes half-yearly results.",SCHEMA,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,fc03d66ef75da373,6e6626d8e0f6b007,,,fc03d66ef75da373,6e6626d8e0f6b007,,,,,HV0153,9bdadc01ea707d39,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

ce0341239bea4a0c,"If a firm is an international bank or a UK trading bank, what does it need to do with its booking arrangements to meet the PRA’s expectations on prudent conduct of business and on risk management and resolvability, and how does the PRA’s proportional approach based on the firm’s investment banking or sales and trading activity affect what is expected?","If the firm is an international bank or a UK trading bank, the PRA’s expectations for booking arrangements apply to it, and the PRA will apply those expectations in a way that is proportionate to the level of investment banking or sales and trading activity the firm undertakes [#SRC:8a9b8ceafce61236]. Within that scope, the firm should organise its booking arrangements so they help it meet the threshold condition on the prudent conduct of business and support the organisational requirements relating to risk management and resolvability that the PRA links to booking-arrangements organisation [#TGT:9efcdb7da1784680]. The firm should also be prepared to notify the PRA when it plans material changes to its booking arrangements that could affect how its risk management operates, because the PRA expects firms to inform it in those circumstances [#TGT:9efcdb7da1784680]. In practice, this means the firm should treat the booking-arrangements expectations as applicable across both bank types, but calibrate how it implements and evidences them in line with the scale of its relevant activities, while still ensuring the arrangements are organised to support prudent conduct, risk management, and resolvability outcomes and that material, risk-management-impacting changes are communicated to the PRA [#SRC:8a9b8ceafce61236] [#TGT:9efcdb7da1784680].","The expectations of a firm’s booking arrangements set out in this section are applicable to all international banks and UK trading banks. Paragraphs 4.24A - 4.25Z and 4.25AE are applicable to both types of bank, paragraphs 4.25AA - 4.25AD are applicable only to international banks [see para 1.1 ]. The PRA will apply these expectations in a manner that is proportionate to the level of investment banking or sales and trading activity that the firm undertakes.","The PRA has a number of expectations concerning how international banks and UK trading banks should organise their booking arrangements in order to meet the threshold condition on the prudent conduct of business, their obligations under Fundamental Rules 3 , 5 , 6 and 8 , and under the General Organisational Requirements (GOR) relating to risk management and resolvability. The PRA also has an expectation under Fundamental Rule 7 and General Notification Requirement 2.3(1) that a firm should inform the PRA when it plans to make material changes to its booking arrangements that could impact how its risk management operates.",SCHEMA,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,8a9b8ceafce61236,9efcdb7da1784680,,,8a9b8ceafce61236,9efcdb7da1784680,,,,,HV0154,ce0341239bea4a0c,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

2e91d3f27b049457,"If you are checking whether eligible own funds cover the minimum consolidated group SCR, do you have to calculate group solvency using the participating undertaking’s proportional share in its related undertakings, and does this sit within the principles that apply with any necessary changes?","Yes. The check on whether eligible own funds qualify to cover the minimum consolidated group SCR is a specific determination that must be made by applying the relevant principles with any necessary changes, and it also requires that the group solvency calculation be done in the required way [#SRC:62d005c6aa11116b]. That required way includes taking account of the proportional share held by the participating undertaking in its related undertakings when calculating the solvency of the group [#TGT:acc84032d208c7bc]. So, when you perform the solvency calculation that underpins the coverage assessment, you must reflect the participating undertaking’s proportional share rather than treating all related undertakings as if they were fully owned or fully included without adjustment. Because the proportional-share approach is a mandatory element of the group solvency calculation, it directly influences the outcome of the determination about whether the eligible own funds are sufficient to cover the minimum consolidated group SCR. The overall obligation is therefore to combine (i) the adapted application of the relevant principles for the coverage determination and (ii) the proportional-share treatment within the group solvency calculation used for that determination [#SRC:62d005c6aa11116b] [#TGT:acc84032d208c7bc].","(3) For the purposes of determining whether those eligible own funds qualify to cover the minimum consolidated group SCR of a group , the principles in 8 to 10 apply with any necessary changes. Undertakings In Difficulty 3 also applies with any necessary changes.",The calculation of the solvency of a group must take account of the proportional share held by the participating undertaking in its related undertakings .,SCHEMA,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,62d005c6aa11116b,acc84032d208c7bc,,,62d005c6aa11116b,acc84032d208c7bc,,,,,HV0155,2e91d3f27b049457,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

297d3cdba76c800a,"If the originator is the only investor in the securitisation, can the firm treat the required information as already made available by sending it in internal reports to committees or the management board, and what still must be made available to holders of a securitisation position, to the PRA, and (if asked) to potential investors?","Yes, in the specific situation where the originator is also the sole investor in the transaction, the PRA expects the firm may treat the relevant information as “made available” to investors through internal reporting to appropriate committees or the management board, as long as that reporting includes the required information [#SRC:8db7bd9adb490bd7]. However, this does not replace the wider requirement that the originator, sponsor and SSPE of a securitisation must make at least specified information available to holders of a securitisation position and to the PRA, and must also make it available to potential investors when they request it [#TGT:7a03dc40aca6d810]. So, even if internal reporting is used to cover the investor side in this sole-investor scenario, the firm still needs to ensure the information is actually available for the other audiences named, including the PRA and any potential investors who ask for it. The internal reports should therefore be prepared and maintained in a way that preserves the required content for those availability purposes.","Where the originator is also the sole investor in the transaction, the PRA expects that the firm may consider the information specified in Article 7(1)(a) and (e) of Chapter 2 of the Securitisation Part of the PRA Rulebook as ‘made available’ to investors through internal reporting to appropriate committees or the management board, provided the reporting contains the required information.","The originator , sponsor and SSPE of a securitisation shall, in accordance with paragraph 2 of this Article and Chapters 5 and 6 , make at least the following information available to holders of a securitisation position , to the PRA and, upon request, to potential investors :",SCHEMA,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,8db7bd9adb490bd7,7a03dc40aca6d810,,,8db7bd9adb490bd7,7a03dc40aca6d810,,,,,HV0156,297d3cdba76c800a,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

bd627327d816cbb3,"If the parent insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company has issued subordinated debt (or has other eligible own funds that are limited), and the Solvency II undertakings in the group are subsidiaries of that holding company, where must the group solvency calculation be done and what method must be used?","If the parent insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company has issued subordinated debt or has other eligible own funds that are subject to the stated limits, then the group supervision provisions apply for the purpose of applying the relevant provisions in that situation [#SRC:98bb2cbec557bb21]. When, in addition, the Solvency II undertakings in the group are subsidiary undertakings of an insurance holding company or a mixed financial holding company, the group’s solvency calculation is not optional: it must be carried out at the level of the insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company, and it must be done using the specified calculation approach that is required to be applied for that calculation [#TGT:bfadda41c802247a]. Read together, these requirements mean that the presence of subordinated debt or other limited eligible own funds at the parent holding company level triggers the application of the group supervision provisions, and the group solvency calculation must then be performed at the holding-company level for groups where the Solvency II undertakings sit as subsidiaries under that holding company [#SRC:98bb2cbec557bb21] [#TGT:bfadda41c802247a].","For the purposes of applying the provisions set out in 14.1 , where the parent insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company has issued subordinated debt or has other eligible own funds subject to the limits set out in Own Funds 4 and 4A , Group Supervision 10.3 shall apply.","(1) Where Solvency II undertakings in a group are subsidiary undertakings of an insurance holding company or a mixed financial holding company , the calculation of the solvency of the group must be carried out at the level of the insurance holding company or mixed financial holding company applying 7.1(2) to 12 .",SCHEMA,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,98bb2cbec557bb21,bfadda41c802247a,,,98bb2cbec557bb21,bfadda41c802247a,,,,,HV0157,bd627327d816cbb3,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

a8372d3ee3c21c8e,"If a firm must be able to identify eligible deposits immediately, can it do this by marking the eligible depositor’s account that holds the eligible deposits, and does it need to remove that marker if the account balance is zero or goes negative?","A firm must mark eligible deposits so they can be identified immediately. To meet that requirement, the PRA considers it acceptable for the firm to achieve the marking by marking the accounts of eligible depositors that contain eligible deposits, rather than needing a different method that marks each deposit separately. This means an account-level marker can be used as the practical way to ensure eligible deposits are identifiable without delay, as long as it results in immediate identification of the eligible deposits. The PRA also clarifies what to do when the marked account does not show a positive balance: if the account has a nil balance, or if its balance becomes negative, the PRA does not expect firms to remove the eligible deposit marker. So, the firm can keep the marker on the account even when the balance is zero or below zero, while still maintaining the overall capability to identify eligible deposits immediately through its marking approach. [#TGT:60b306349873ce31] [#SRC:91baf6dd072390d5]","For the purposes of meeting Depositor Protection 11.1 , the PRA considers the marking of eligible deposits may be achieved by marking accounts of eligible depositors which contain eligible deposits. For the avoidance of doubt, where such an account has a nil balance, or the balance becomes negative, the PRA does not expect firms to remove the eligible deposit marker.",A firm must mark eligible deposits in a way that allows for the immediate identification of such deposits .,SCHEMA,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,91baf6dd072390d5,60b306349873ce31,,,91baf6dd072390d5,60b306349873ce31,,,,,HV0158,a8372d3ee3c21c8e,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

e750569339971059,"Each year when the PRA sets O-SII buffer rates using the Financial Policy Committee’s framework, what number does it base the rates on, and what changed from the earlier method once the updated framework took effect?","The PRA sets O-SII buffer rates annually by applying the Financial Policy Committee (FPC) framework for setting those rates, and under that framework the rates are determined based on firms’ UK leverage exposure measure [#SRC:68b4e61f2c4a680e]. The updated FPC framework is effective from 2023, which means that from that point the PRA’s annual rate-setting should use the UK leverage exposure measure as the basis for determining the rates [#TGT:8dbe00ff83963038]. This represents a change from the earlier method: before the updated framework took effect, rates were determined based on firms’ total assets [#TGT:8dbe00ff83963038]. So, to apply the procedure correctly, you need to align the PRA’s annual setting of O-SII buffer rates with the applicable version of the FPC framework—using total assets for the earlier approach and using the UK leverage exposure measure under the updated framework effective from 2023 [#SRC:68b4e61f2c4a680e] [#TGT:8dbe00ff83963038].","The PRA notes that O-SII designation does not automatically result in higher loss absorbency requirements in the form of an O-SII buffer or otherwise. An O-SII buffer can only apply to O-SIIs or part of an O-SII that are ring-fenced bodies (RFBs) or large building societies. The Financial Policy Committee (FPC) maintains the framework for setting O-SII buffer rates, 5 according to which, O-SII buffer rates are determined based on firms’ UK leverage exposure measure. 6 The PRA sets O-SII buffer rates annually based on the FPC’s framework. The PRA has separately set out its approach in applying the FPC’s framework. 7","6. As per updated FPC framework, effective from 2023. Prior to this, rates were determined based on firms' total assets.",SCHEMA,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,68b4e61f2c4a680e,8dbe00ff83963038,,,68b4e61f2c4a680e,8dbe00ff83963038,,,,,HV0159,e750569339971059,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

2717edd29bf59cea,"If a firm cannot show that its operational arrangements support recovery and resolution, what does the PRA expect the firm to change, and what must the firm be able to explain about critical services if the Bank uses its stabilisation powers (as defined)?","If a firm cannot demonstrate how its operational arrangements facilitate recovery and resolution, the PRA expects the firm to make changes so that its operational arrangements achieve that recovery-and-resolution outcome [#SRC:69a8d0afb1f8c2dd]. Deciding whether the firm has met this expectation involves supervisory judgement, but there is a minimum requirement the firm must meet. At a minimum, the PRA expects the firm to be able to describe what would happen to its critical services in two situations: (1) if the firm’s recovery options were executed, and (2) if the Bank were to apply one or more of its stabilisation powers [#SRC:69a8d0afb1f8c2dd]. The stabilisation powers the firm must consider are the Bank’s stabilisation powers set out in the Banking Act 2009 [#TGT:784dbf1f736c397d]. So, the firm’s explanation needs to cover the impact on critical services both when recovery options are used and when the Bank applies those Banking Act stabilisation powers, and the firm should change its operational arrangements if it cannot demonstrate they support recovery and resolution [#SRC:69a8d0afb1f8c2dd] [#TGT:784dbf1f736c397d].","If a firm cannot demonstrate how its operational arrangements facilitate recovery and resolution, the PRA expects the firm to make changes to achieve this outcome. Supervisory judgement will be required to assess this but, as a minimum, the PRA expects firms to be able to describe what would happen to critical services if recovery options were executed or if the Bank were to apply one or more of its stabilisation powers 13 . This includes the examples listed below, where relevant:",13. The Bank’s stabilisation powers are set out in s.1(4) of the Banking Act 2009.,SCHEMA,,basic,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,69a8d0afb1f8c2dd,784dbf1f736c397d,,,69a8d0afb1f8c2dd,784dbf1f736c397d,,,,,HV0160,2717edd29bf59cea,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

bf6a9dc9268517bb,"When smaller firms (Category 3-4 PRA regulated firms) set remuneration policies, what must they do to apply proportionality without disapplying the relevant requirements for Solvency II staff, while also ensuring the policy design reflects the firm’s internal organisation and the nature, scale and complexity of the risks in its business?","Smaller firms (Category 3-4 PRA regulated firms) must approach remuneration policy setting on the basis that proportionality affects how requirements are applied, not whether they apply. In practice, they are expected to comply appropriately when setting remuneration policies and must not treat proportionality as a basis to disapply the applicable requirements; instead, they should exercise appropriate judgement so that the specific arrangements for Solvency II staff are applied proportionately and modified where required to reflect the size and nature of their businesses [#SRC:a1a186c5cfc66eed]. At the same time, the firm must ensure the remuneration policy is designed to take into account its internal organisation and the nature, scale and complexity of the risks inherent in its business [#TGT:07a05eb1c221e73c]. Read together, this means the firm should calibrate and, where necessary, adjust Solvency II staff arrangements in a way that remains compliant, while explicitly aligning the policy’s structure and operation with how the firm is organised and with the risk profile and complexity of its activities, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.",The PRA will still expect smaller firms (Category 3-4 PRA regulated firms) to comply appropriately with Chapter 3A when setting their remuneration policies. The application of proportionality under Conditions Governing Business 3A.3 does not equate to smaller firms being able to disapply the Chapter 3A requirements. These firms should be exercising appropriate judgement to ensure that the specific arrangements for Solvency II staff contained in Conditions Governing Business 3A.2 are applied proportionality and modified where required to reflect the size and nature of their businesses.,"A firm must ensure that the remuneration policy is designed in such a way as to take into account the internal organisation of the firm , and the nature, scale and complexity of the risks inherent in its business.",SCHEMA,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,a1a186c5cfc66eed,07a05eb1c221e73c,,,a1a186c5cfc66eed,07a05eb1c221e73c,,,,,HV0161,bf6a9dc9268517bb,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,

4ba77d22298eb93f,"Where a Northern Ireland credit union has a loan that was outstanding on 31 March 2012 and continues to be repayable under the loan agreement terms in effect on that date, how does the permission not to comply with certain requirements interact with the obligation to maintain a minimum capital-to-total-assets ratio when the credit union is owed by a member more than £7,500 in excess of the member’s attached shares (or is owed by another credit union more than £7,500)?","A Northern Ireland credit union is permitted not to comply with the specified set of requirements in relation to a loan that was outstanding on 31 March 2012, but only on the condition that the loan continues to be repayable in accordance with the terms of the relevant loan agreement that were in effect on 31 March 2012 [#SRC:b5040d03979336d0]. Separately, where a credit union is owed by a member a total amount greater than £7,500 in excess of the attached shares held by that member, or is owed by another credit union an amount greater than £7,500, it must maintain a capital-to-total-assets ratio of at least 5% [#TGT:14592babb38a22de]. Read together, the permission operates as a limited carve-out tied to the status and repayment terms of the particular pre-existing loan, whereas the capital ratio requirement is framed as a mandatory prudential obligation triggered by the size and nature of amounts owed to the credit union. Accordingly, even if the credit union can rely on the loan-related permission for the qualifying outstanding loan, it still must ensure it maintains at least the 5% capital-to-total-assets ratio whenever the stated £7,500 threshold condition is met [#SRC:b5040d03979336d0] [#TGT:14592babb38a22de].",A Northern Ireland credit union need not comply with 3.2 to 3.9 with respect to any loan outstanding on 31 March 2012 provided that the loan remains repayable in accordance with the terms of the relevant loan agreement in effect on 31 March 2012.,"A credit union that is owed by a member a total amount greater than £7,500 in excess of the attached shares held by that member , or by another credit union an amount greater than £7,500, must maintain a capital -to- total-assets ratio of at least 5%.",SCHEMA,,professional,UKFIN,mixed_difficulty,b5040d03979336d0,14592babb38a22de,,,b5040d03979336d0,14592babb38a22de,,,,,HV0162,4ba77d22298eb93f,ObliQA-XRef_Out_Datasets/final_large_merged/ObliQA-XRef-UKFIN-ALL/final.jsonl,,,,
